  • Custom code: for APIs the pattern inference does not cover

docs.title: Endpoint types
docs.text:
Endpoints are the main building blocks of TypedRest. An endpoint represents an URI that provides methods for interacting with a specific resource. The type of the endpoint determines the available methods. An endpoint can also provide child endpoints (represent child URIs) via composition.

TypedRest provides a number of endpoint types modelling common REST patterns. Most APIs can be consumed by either directly using these types or by deriving from them and adding additional methods for special use cases.

Entry endpoints represent the top-level URI of APIs.

Generic endpoints allow you to model collections and elements:

  • Element endpoint - individual resource (read, write, delete)
  • Collection endpoint - collection of entities addressable as elements (read all, create, get child by ID)
  • Indexer endpoint - address child endpoints by ID

RPC endpoints allow you to interact with non-RESTful resources that act like callable functions:

  • Action endpoint - no input or output
  • Consumer endpoint - takes entity as input
  • Producer endpoint - produces entity as output
  • Function endpoint - takes entity as input and produces entity as output

Raw endpoints allow you to transmit binary data rather than serialized objects:

  • Upload endpoint - accept binary uploads
  • Blob endpoint - download or upload a binary blob

Reactive endpoints allow you to receive data as push streams rather than explicitly pulling:

  • Polling endpoint - poll resource for state changes
  • Streaming endpoint - stream of entities via persistent connection
  • SSE endpoint - stream of entities via Server-Sent Events
  • Streaming Collection endpoint - collection of entities observable as append-only stream

docs.title: Allowed methods
docs.text:
Endpoints record the Allow header of each response. Afterwards you can check on the same endpoint object whether the server permits an operation, for example to hide a delete button instead of handling 403 Forbidden after the fact. The value is null/undefined as long as the server has not said.

Endpoint .NET Java/Kotlin TypeScript Element SetAllowed, MergeAllowed, DeleteAllowed isSetAllowed, isMergeAllowed, isDeleteAllowed setAllowed, mergeAllowed, deleteAllowed Collection ReadAllAllowed, ReadRangeAllowed, CreateAllowed, CreateAllAllowed, SetAllAllowed readAllAllowed, readRangeAllowed, createAllowed, createAllAllowed, setAllAllowed readAllAllowed, readRangeAllowed, createAllowed, createAllAllowed, setAllAllowed RPC InvokeAllowed isInvokeAllowed invokeAllowed Blob DownloadAllowed, UploadAllowed, DeleteAllowed isDownloadAllowed, isUploadAllowed, isDeleteAllowed downloadAllowed, uploadAllowed, deleteAllowed

The Java/Kotlin names are the Kotlin property names; Java calls them as getters, e.g. isDeleteAllowed() and getCreateAllowed().

ReadRangeAllowed comes from the Accept-Ranges header rather than Allow. RPC and blob endpoints have nothing to read before they are used, so they offer a probe method (ProbeAsync()/probe()) that sends an OPTIONS request to fill in these values.

docs.title: Referrers
docs.text: The constructors of all endpoints (except entry endpoints) take a referrer parameter. This is used to inherit relative URI bases, serializers and error handling.

docs.title: Entry endpoint
docs.text:
Represent the top-level URI of an API. Used to address the various resources of the API.

The constructor of the entry endpoint requires you to specify the APIs root URL. It also provides optional parameters to override the default HTTP client, JSON serializer, error handler and link handler.

docs.title: Usage
HTTP client
docs.text:
Every endpoint sends its requests through the HTTP client of the entry endpoint it was created from. Configure that HTTP client, for example with a timeout or default headers, and the configuration applies to every request of the client.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

Pass your own HttpClient, or change the one the entry endpoint created via its HttpClient property:

var client = new EntryEndpoint(new HttpClient { Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30) }, new Uri("http://example.com/api/"));
client.HttpClient.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("X-Api-Key", apiKey);

If you omit the URI, the HttpClient's BaseAddress is used instead. In applications that use IServiceCollection, let IHttpClientFactory create the HttpClient; see Dependency injection.

TypedRest for the JVM uses OkHttp. Pass a configured OkHttpClient, and add headers with an interceptor:

OkHttpClient httpClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .addInterceptor(chain -> chain.proceed(chain.request().newBuilder()
        .header("X-Api-Key", apiKey)
        .build()))
    .build();
EntryEndpoint client = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/api/"), httpClient, new JacksonJsonSerializer());

If you use streaming or SSE endpoints, avoid callTimeout(): it limits the entire call, including reading the response body, so it cuts off long-lived streams. readTimeout() (10 seconds by default) limits the time between two reads, so a stream that stays silent for longer is cut off as well.

TypedRest for the JVM uses OkHttp. Pass a configured OkHttpClient, and add headers with an interceptor:

val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .addInterceptor { chain ->
        chain.proceed(chain.request().newBuilder()
            .header("X-Api-Key", apiKey)
            .build())
    }
    .build()
val client = EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/api/"), httpClient)

If you use streaming or SSE endpoints, avoid callTimeout(): it limits the entire call, including reading the response body, so it cuts off long-lived streams. readTimeout() (10 seconds by default) limits the time between two reads, so a stream that stays silent for longer is cut off as well.

Set default headers on the entry endpoint's httpClient:

const client = new EntryEndpoint(new URL("http://example.com/api/"));
client.httpClient.defaultHeaders.set("X-Api-Key", apiKey);

To change how requests are sent, pass your own implementation of HttpClient as the fifth constructor argument, for example a class derived from FetchHttpClient.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Since all requests go through the entry endpoint's HTTP client, authentication is configured there too.

docs.title: HTTP Basic authentication
API keys and bearer tokens
docs.text: Send a fixed key or token as a default header, for example Authorization: Bearer ... or X-Api-Key: ....

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
Tokens from an OAuth 2.0 identity server expire, so the client has to request them, reuse them while they are valid and renew them.

  • In .NET, the TypedRest.OAuth package does this for the client credentials flow.
  • TypedRest for the JVM and for TypeScript have no built-in OAuth support. Add the token with an OkHttp interceptor or an HttpClient derived from FetchHttpClient; the Authentication tutorial shows both.

A rejected request throws an AuthenticationException/AuthenticationError (401) or an authorization exception (403); see Exception mapping.

docs.title: Collection endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint for a collection of entities addressable as Element endpoints.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Get ID / Entity Endpoint - Get an Element endpoint for a specific child element. Read all - Entities GET Returns all entities in the collection. Read range Range Entities GET Returns all entities within a specific range of the collection. Create Entity - POST Adds an entity as a new element to the collection. Create All Entities - PATCH Adds (or updates) multiple entities as elements in the collection. Set All Entities - PUT Replaces the entire content of the collection with new entities.

Extends Indexer endpoint

docs.title: Usage
Element endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint for an individual resource.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Exists - Boolean HEAD Determines whether the element currently exists. Read - Entity GET Returns the entity. Set Entity Entity PUT Sets/replaces the entity. Merge Entity Entity PATCH Modifies the existing entity by merging changes. Delete - - DELETE Deletes the element.

docs.title: Usage
Indexer endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint that addresses child endpoints by ID.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Get ID Endpoint - Get an Element endpoint for a specific child element.

docs.title: Usage
Blob endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint for a binary blob that can be downloaded or uploaded.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Download - Binary data GET Downloads the blob's content. Upload Binary data - PUT Uploads content for the blob.

docs.title: Usage
Upload endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint that accepts binary uploads.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Upload Binary data - POST Uploads data to the endpoint.

docs.title: Usage
Reactive endpoints
docs.text:
Reactive endpoints turn repeated or long-running HTTP requests into a stream of entities, so you get notified of changes instead of reading a resource once.

  • Polling endpoint - poll a resource for state changes
  • Streaming Collection endpoint - follow a collection that is only ever appended to
  • SSE endpoint - receive events pushed by the server as Server-Sent Events
  • Streaming endpoint - receive entities the server writes into a persistent connection

Packages

For .NET, add the TypedRest.Reactive NuGet package. For Java/Kotlin, add the typedrest-reactive Maven artifact. In TypeScript, reactive endpoints are part of the main typedrest package.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
.NET and Java/Kotlin provide streams as ReactiveX observables via GetObservable()/getObservable(). TypeScript provides them as async iterables via stream().

Nothing is sent until you subscribe to the observable or start iterating.

docs.title: Stopping a stream
Choosing an endpoint
docs.text:
Polling Streaming collection SSE Streaming Delivers changed states of one resource new elements of a collection events entities Transport repeated GET repeated GET with Range one long-lived GET one long-lived GET Server requirements none range requests SSE output line-separated output Delay up to one polling interval up to one polling interval immediate immediate Resuming not needed by start index by Last-Event-ID not supported Good for job status, slow-changing state logs, feeds, message histories notifications, live dashboards simple feeds you don't control

As a rule of thumb: use polling if you cannot change the server, a streaming collection if the data is a list that only grows and clients need to catch up on what they missed, and SSE if updates must arrive immediately.

Long-lived connections need some care in your infrastructure: proxies and load balancers may close idle connections or buffer responses. The SSE endpoint reconnects for you, but disable response buffering on the server side for streamed responses such as text/event-stream.

The Live updates tutorial uses polling, a streaming collection and SSE for different parts of one API.

docs.title: Polling endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint for a resource that can be polled for state changes.

Note

For .NET, use the TypedRest.Reactive NuGet package. For Java/Kotlin, use the typedrest-reactive Maven artifact. For TypeScript, reactive endpoints are part of the main typedrest package and provide AsyncIterables via stream() instead of observables.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Get stream - Entity stream GET Provides a stream of entity states. Exists - Boolean HEAD Determines whether the element currently exists. Read - Entity GET Returns the entity. Set Entity Entity PUT Sets/replaces the entity. Merge Entity Entity PATCH Modifies the existing entity by merging changes. Delete - - DELETE Deletes the element.

Extends Element endpoint

docs.title: Usage
End condition
docs.text:
Pass an end condition to the constructor to stop polling once the entity reaches its final state. The stream emits that final state and then completes:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var job = new PollingEndpoint<Job>(client, "jobs/42", endCondition: x => x.State == "completed");

PollingEndpoint<Job> job = new PollingEndpointImpl<>(client, "jobs/42", Job.class, x -> x.getState().equals("completed"));

val job = PollingEndpointImpl(client, "jobs/42", Job::class.java) { it.state == "completed" }

const job = new PollingEndpoint<Job>(client, "jobs/42", x => x.state === "completed");

Without an end condition, the stream continues until you stop it.

docs.title: Change detection
docs.text:
States identical to the previous one are skipped, so the stream only delivers changes.

.NET and Java/Kotlin compare states with Equals/equals. Give the entity class value equality (a C# record, a Kotlin data class, or overridden equals in Java); otherwise every poll deserializes a new, unequal object and counts as a change. TypeScript compares the serialized JSON.

This also applies to DTOs from the code generator: generated Kotlin DTOs are data classes, but generated C# and Java DTOs are plain classes without value equality. Add Equals/GetHashCode in a partial class (C#), or poll with a hand-written entity class (Java).

docs.title: Polling interval
docs.text:
The endpoint waits 3 seconds between requests by default. Change this with PollingInterval/pollingInterval (a TimeSpan in .NET, a Duration in Java/Kotlin, milliseconds in TypeScript).

The server can slow clients down: if a response has a Retry-After header, the endpoint uses it as the new polling interval.

docs.title: SSE endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint for a stream of entities using Server-Sent Events (SSE).

Note

For .NET, use the TypedRest.Reactive NuGet package. For Java/Kotlin, use the typedrest-reactive Maven artifact. For TypeScript, reactive endpoints are part of the main typedrest package and provide AsyncIterables via stream() instead of observables.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Get stream - Entity stream GET Provides a stream of entities.

The request is sent with Accept: text/event-stream. The data: field of each event is deserialized as an entity. Unlike the Streaming endpoint, which simply splits the response body on a separator, this understands the SSE wire format, so it can also make use of the event type, id and reconnection interval the server sends along.

docs.title: Usage
Event types
docs.text:
A server can label events with an event: field to send more than one kind of message over a single stream. Pass an event type to the constructor to receive only those events; all others are ignored. Leave it unset to receive every event, whatever its type.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var updates = new SseStreamingEndpoint<Job>(client, "jobs/events", eventType: "update");

StreamingEndpoint<Job> updates = new SseStreamingEndpointImpl<>(client, "jobs/events", Job.class, "update");

val updates = SseStreamingEndpointImpl(client, "jobs/events", Job::class.java, eventType = "update")

const updates = new SseStreamingEndpoint<Job>(client, "jobs/events", "update");

docs.title: Reconnecting
docs.text:
Long-lived streams can get interrupted. By default the endpoint reconnects on its own after a dropped connection, a transient transport error or a 5xx response, without the consumer seeing anything.

Two SSE fields steer this. A retry: field tells the client how long to wait before reconnecting; until the server sends one, the endpoint waits three seconds. An id: field is remembered and sent back as a Last-Event-ID header on the next attempt, so a server that supports it can resume where the stream left off rather than starting over.

To end a stream for good, respond with 204 No Content. The stream then completes instead of reconnecting.

Turn reconnecting off to have connection failures surface as errors instead:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var events = new SseStreamingEndpoint<Event>(client, "events")
{
    AutoReconnect = false
};

SseStreamingEndpointImpl<Event> events = new SseStreamingEndpointImpl<>(client, "events", Event.class, null);
events.setAutoReconnect(false);

val events = SseStreamingEndpointImpl(client, "events", Event::class.java)
    .apply { autoReconnect = false }

const events = new SseStreamingEndpoint<Event>(client, "events");
events.autoReconnect = false;

docs.title: Server requirements
docs.text:
The server responds with Content-Type: text/event-stream and writes events into the open response as they happen:

id: 17
event: updated
data: {"type":"updated","contact":{"id":"1337","name":"Smith"}}

Proxies and load balancers may buffer responses or close idle connections. Disable response buffering for text/event-stream on the server side; the endpoint takes care of reconnecting.

docs.title: Streaming Collection endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint for a collection of entities observable as an append-only stream using long-polling.

Note

For .NET, use the TypedRest.Reactive NuGet package. For Java/Kotlin, use the typedrest-reactive Maven artifact. For TypeScript, reactive endpoints are part of the main typedrest package and provide AsyncIterables via stream() instead of observables.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Get stream - Entity stream GET Provides a stream of elements. Get ID / Entity Endpoint - Get an Element endpoint for a specific child element. Read all - Entities GET Returns all entities in the collection. Read range Range Entities GET Returns all entities within a specific range of the collection. Create Entity - POST Adds an entity as a new element to the collection. Create All Entities - PATCH Adds (or updates) multiple entities as elements in the collection. Set All Entities - PUT Replaces the entire content of the collection with new entities.

Extends Collection endpoint

docs.title: Usage
Start index
docs.text:
Pass a start index to skip elements you have already seen, which lets a client resume where it left off, or a negative one to start with the last few. Zero, the default, starts with the first element.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
// Start after the first 10 elements
messages.GetObservable(startIndex: 10);

// Start with the last 5 elements
messages.GetObservable(startIndex: -5);

// Start after the first 10 elements
messages.getObservable(10);

// Start with the last 5 elements
messages.getObservable(-5);

// Start after the first 10 elements
messages.getObservable(10)

// Start with the last 5 elements
messages.getObservable(-5)

// Start after the first 10 elements
messages.stream(10);

// Start with the last 5 elements
messages.stream(-5);

docs.title: Server requirements
docs.text:
The endpoint uses the same HTTP range requests as reading a range of a regular collection, so the server has to support them:

  1. The client requests Range: elements=N-, from the next position it has not seen to the end (or Range: elements=-N for the last N elements).
  2. If there are elements from N on, the server responds with 206 Partial Content, the elements, and Content-Range: elements N-M/*. The client waits for the polling interval and asks for the elements after M.
  3. If there are none yet, the server responds with 416 Range Not Satisfiable. The client waits for the polling interval and asks again.

Leave out the total

Use * for the total in Content-Range, as above. If the server sends a total (elements 0-9/10) and the response reaches it, the client takes that as the end of the collection and the stream completes.

The polling interval is 3 seconds by default. Change it with PollingInterval/pollingInterval (a TimeSpan in .NET, a Duration in Java/Kotlin, milliseconds in TypeScript). If a response has a Retry-After header, the endpoint uses it as the new polling interval.

docs.title: Streaming endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint for a stream of entities using a persistent HTTP connection. The entities the server writes into the open response body are split on a configurable separator, \n by default, as in newline-delimited JSON. If the server speaks the Server-Sent Events protocol instead, use the SSE endpoint.

Unlike the SSE endpoint, this has no event types, event IDs or automatic reconnecting. Proxies and load balancers may buffer responses or close idle connections, so disable response buffering for the stream on the server side.

Note

For .NET, use the TypedRest.Reactive NuGet package. For Java/Kotlin, use the typedrest-reactive Maven artifact. For TypeScript, reactive endpoints are part of the main typedrest package and provide AsyncIterables via stream() instead of observables.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Get stream - Entity stream GET Provides a stream of entities.

docs.title: Usage
Action endpoint
docs.text:
RPC endpoint that is invoked with no input or output.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Invoke - - POST Invokes the action.

docs.title: Usage
Consumer endpoint
docs.text:
RPC endpoint that takes an entity as input when invoked.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Invoke Entity - POST Sends the entity to the consumer.

docs.title: Usage
Function endpoint
docs.text:
RPC endpoint that takes an entity as input and returns another entity as output when invoked.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Invoke Entity Entity POST Invokes the function.

docs.title: Usage
Producer endpoint
docs.text:
RPC endpoint that returns an entity as output when invoked.

Method Input Result HTTP Verb Description Invoke - Entity POST Gets an entity from the producer.

docs.title: Usage
Exception mapping
docs.text:
TypedRest maps non-success HTTP Status (4xx and 5xx) to exceptions/errors. The following mappings are applied by default:

HTTP Status Code .NET Exception Java/Kotlin Exception TypeScript Error 400 Bad Request InvalidDataException BadRequestException BadRequestError 401 Unauthorized AuthenticationException AuthenticationException AuthenticationError 403 Forbidden UnauthorizedAccessException AuthorizationException AuthorizationError 404 NotFound or 410 Gone KeyNotFoundException NotFoundException NotFoundError 408 Request Timeout TimeoutException TimeoutException TimeoutError 409 Conflict InvalidOperationException ConflictException ConflictError 412 Precondition Failed InvalidOperationException ConflictException ConcurrencyError 416 Range Not Satisfiable InvalidOperationException ConflictException RangeNotSatisfiableError other HttpRequestException HttpException HttpError

docs.title: Link handling
docs.text:
TypedRest supports a variety of different ways to establish links between endpoints:

  • Hard-coded relative URIs
  • URI templates for dynamic URL construction
  • Links via HTTP Link Header transmitted in response headers
  • Links encoded in resources via HAL for hypermedia-driven APIs

docs.title: Link resolution
docs.text:
All endpoints provide methods for resolving links:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
// Resolves all links with a specific relation type.
IReadOnlyList<(Uri uri, string? title)> GetLinks(string rel);

// Resolves a single link with a specific relation type.
Uri Link(string rel);

// Resolves a link template with a specific relation type.
Uri LinkTemplate(string rel, IDictionary<string, object> variables);

// Resolves all links with a specific relation type.
List<Pair<URI, String>> getLinks(String rel);

// Resolves a single link with a specific relation type.
URI link(String rel);

// Resolves a link template with a specific relation type.
URI linkTemplate(String rel, Map<String, Object> variables);

// Resolves all links with a specific relation type.
fun getLinks(rel: String): List<Pair<URI, String?>>

// Resolves a single link with a specific relation type.
fun link(rel: String): URI

// Resolves a link template with a specific relation type.
fun linkTemplate(rel: String, variables: Map<String, Any>): URI

// Resolves all links with a specific relation type.
getLinks(rel: string): { uri: URL; title?: string; }[];

// Resolves a single link with a specific relation type.
link(rel: string): URL;

// Resolves a link template with a specific relation type.
linkTemplate(rel: string, variables: { [key: string]: any; }): URL;

These methods use cached data from the last response. On cache miss, they perform a lazy lookup using HTTP HEAD.

docs.title: HAL (Hypertext Application Language)
docs.text: TypedRest supports extracting links from response bodies using the HAL specification. HAL provides a consistent format for embedding links and embedded resources within JSON responses.

docs.title: HAL format
docs.text:
HAL adds a _links object to JSON responses containing links organized by relation type:

{
    "id": 123,
    "name": "John Doe",
    "_links": {
        "self": { "href": "/users/123" },
        "orders": { "href": "/users/123/orders" },
        "search": { "href": "/users/{id}", "templated": true }
    }
}

docs.title: Content type
docs.text:
TypedRest recognizes HAL responses by the application/hal+json content type:

When this content type is present, TypedRest automatically parses the _links object and makes the links available through the standard link resolution methods.

docs.title: Using HAL links
docs.text:
After receiving a HAL response, you can resolve links just like with HTTP Link headers:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
await endpoint.ReadAsync();

// Resolve a single link
Uri ordersUri = endpoint.Link("orders");

// Resolve a templated link
Uri userUri = endpoint.LinkTemplate("search", new { id = "456" });

endpoint.read();

// Resolve a single link
URI ordersUri = endpoint.link("orders");

// Resolve a templated link
URI userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("search", Map.of("id", "456"));

endpoint.read()

// Resolve a single link
val ordersUri = endpoint.link("orders")

// Resolve a templated link
val userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("search", mapOf("id" to "456"))

await endpoint.read();

// Resolve a single link
const ordersUri = endpoint.link("orders");

// Resolve a templated link
const userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("search", { id: "456" });

docs.title: Multiple links
docs.text:
HAL supports multiple links for the same relation type using an array:

{
    "_links": {
        "item": [
            { "href": "/items/1", "title": "First Item" },
            { "href": "/items/2", "title": "Second Item" }
        ]
    }
}

Retrieve all links with GetLinks:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var items = endpoint.GetLinks("item");
foreach (var (uri, title) in items)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{title}: {uri}");
}

List<Link> items = endpoint.getLinks("item");
for (Link link : items) {
    System.out.println(link.getTitle() + ": " + link.getUri());
}

val items = endpoint.getLinks("item")
for (link in items) {
    println("${link.title}: ${link.uri}")
}

const items = endpoint.getLinks("item");
for (const { uri, title } of items) {
    console.log(`${title}: ${uri}`);
}

docs.title: Templated links
docs.text:
HAL links can be marked as templates with the templated property:

{
    "_links": {
        "find": {
            "href": "/users{?name,email}",
            "templated": true
        }
    }
}
C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var findUri = endpoint.LinkTemplate("find", new { name = "John", email = "john@example.com" });
// Result: /users?name=John&email=john%40example.com

URI findUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("find", Map.of("name", "John", "email", "john@example.com"));
// Result: /users?name=John&email=john%40example.com

val findUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("find", mapOf("name" to "John", "email" to "john@example.com"))
// Result: /users?name=John&email=john%40example.com

const findUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("find", { name: "John", email: "john@example.com" });
// Result: /users?name=John&email=john%40example.com

docs.title: HTTP Link header
docs.text: TypedRest can extract links from HTTP Link headers as defined in RFC 8288. This enables HATEOAS-style navigation where the server provides links to related resources in response headers.

docs.title: Header format
docs.text:
The HTTP Link header follows this format:

Link: <target-uri>; rel="relation-type"; title="optional title"

Multiple links can be specified in a single header, separated by commas:

Link: <http://example.com/users>; rel=self, <http://example.com/user/123>; rel=child

docs.title: Extracting links
docs.text:
TypedRest automatically extracts links from response headers after each request. You can then resolve them:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
// Perform a request
await endpoint.ReadAsync();

// Get all links with a specific relation type
var links = endpoint.GetLinks("child");
foreach (var (uri, title) in links)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"URI: {uri}, Title: {title}");
}

// Get a single link
Uri collectionUri = endpoint.Link("next");

// Perform a request
endpoint.read();

// Get all links with a specific relation type
List<Link> links = endpoint.getLinks("child");
for (Link link : links) {
    System.out.println("URI: " + link.getUri() + ", Title: " + link.getTitle());
}

// Get a single link
URI collectionUri = endpoint.link("next");

// Perform a request
endpoint.read()

// Get all links with a specific relation type
val links = endpoint.getLinks("child")
for (link in links) {
    println("URI: ${link.uri}, Title: ${link.title}")
}

// Get a single link
val collectionUri = endpoint.link("next")

// Perform a request
await endpoint.read();

// Get all links with a specific relation type
const links = endpoint.getLinks("child");
for (const { uri, title } of links) {
    console.log(`URI: ${uri}, Title: ${title}`);
}

// Get a single link
const collectionUri = endpoint.link("next");

docs.title: Templated links
docs.text:
TypedRest extends the standard Link header format to support URI templates. Templates are indicated with templated=true:

Link: </users/{id}>; rel=user; templated=true

This is a non-standard extension, but it allows servers to provide dynamic link templates via headers without needing HAL or another hypermedia format in the response body.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
// Server response:
// Link: </users/{id}>; rel=user; templated=true

var userUri = endpoint.LinkTemplate("user", new { id = "123" });
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

// Server response:
// Link: </users/{id}>; rel=user; templated=true

URI userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("user", Map.of("id", "123"));
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

// Server response:
// Link: </users/{id}>; rel=user; templated=true

val userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("user", mapOf("id" to "123"))
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

// Server response:
// Link: </users/{id}>; rel=user; templated=true

const userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("user", { id: "123" });
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

docs.title: Link header attributes
docs.text:
The following attributes are supported:

Attribute Description rel The relation type (required) title Human-readable title for the link (optional) templated Indicates a URI template when set to true (non-standard)

docs.title: Relative URIs
docs.text: The most straightforward way to navigate between endpoints is using hard-coded relative URIs. When creating child endpoints, you pass a relative URI that is resolved against the parent endpoint's URI.

docs.title: Basic usage
Trailing slash pattern
docs.text:
Standard URI resolution can be tricky when the parent URI doesn't have a trailing slash. Consider:

  • Base URI: http://example.com/endpoint
  • Relative URI: subresource
  • Standard resolution: http://example.com/subresource (replaces endpoint)

This is often not the desired behavior. TypedRest provides a non-standard ./ prefix pattern to handle this:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var parent = new ElementEndpoint<MyEntity>(client, "endpoint");
// parent.Uri = http://example.com/endpoint

// Without ./ prefix - replaces last segment
var child1 = new ActionEndpoint(parent, "subresource");
// child1.Uri = http://example.com/subresource

// With ./ prefix - appends to path
var child2 = new ActionEndpoint(parent, "./subresource");
// child2.Uri = http://example.com/endpoint/subresource

ElementEndpoint<MyEntity> parent = new ElementEndpointImpl<>(client, "endpoint", MyEntity.class);
// parent.getUri() = http://example.com/endpoint

// Without ./ prefix - replaces last segment
ActionEndpoint child1 = new ActionEndpointImpl(parent, "subresource");
// child1.getUri() = http://example.com/subresource

// With ./ prefix - appends to path
ActionEndpoint child2 = new ActionEndpointImpl(parent, "./subresource");
// child2.getUri() = http://example.com/endpoint/subresource

val parent = ElementEndpointImpl(client, "endpoint", MyEntity::class.java)
// parent.uri = http://example.com/endpoint

// Without ./ prefix - replaces last segment
val child1 = ActionEndpointImpl(parent, "subresource")
// child1.uri = http://example.com/subresource

// With ./ prefix - appends to path
val child2 = ActionEndpointImpl(parent, "./subresource")
// child2.uri = http://example.com/endpoint/subresource

const parent = new ElementEndpoint<MyEntity>(client, "endpoint");
// parent.uri = http://example.com/endpoint

// Without ./ prefix - replaces last segment
const child1 = new ActionEndpoint(parent, "subresource");
// child1.uri = http://example.com/subresource

// With ./ prefix - appends to path
const child2 = new ActionEndpoint(parent, "./subresource");
// child2.uri = http://example.com/endpoint/subresource

The ./ prefix tells TypedRest to ensure a trailing slash on the parent URI before resolving the relative URI. This makes the relative URI resolution behave as if the parent URI was http://example.com/endpoint/.

docs.title: Default links
docs.text:
You can also register default links that will be used when the server doesn't provide links for a specific relation type:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
class MyEndpoint : EndpointBase
{
    public MyEndpoint(IEndpoint referrer, string relativeUri) 
        : base(referrer, relativeUri)
    {
        SetDefaultLink("related", "./related-resource");
    }
}

class MyEndpoint extends AbstractEndpoint {
    public MyEndpoint(Endpoint referrer, String relativeUri) {
        super(referrer, relativeUri);
        setDefaultLink("related", "./related-resource");
    }
}

class MyEndpoint(referrer: Endpoint, relativeUri: String) : AbstractEndpoint(referrer, relativeUri) {
    init {
        setDefaultLink("related", "./related-resource")
    }
}

class MyEndpoint extends Endpoint {
    constructor(referrer: Endpoint, relativeUri: string) {
        super(referrer, relativeUri);
        this.setDefaultLink("related", "./related-resource");
    }
}

docs.title: URI templates
docs.text: TypedRest supports URI templates as defined in RFC 6570. URI templates allow you to construct URIs dynamically by substituting variables into a template string.

docs.title: How URI templates work
docs.text:
A URI template contains placeholders (variables) that are replaced with actual values at runtime. For example:

  • Template: /users/{id} with {id: "123"} → /users/123
  • Template: /search{?q,limit} with {q: "test", limit: 10} → /search?q=test&limit=10

docs.title: Server-provided templates
docs.text:
The server can provide URI templates via the HTTP Link header:

Link: </users/{id}>; rel=user; templated=true

Or in HAL:

{
    "_links": {
        "user": {
            "href": "/users/{id}",
            "templated": true
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Resolving templates
docs.text:
Use the LinkTemplate method to resolve a template with variables:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
// After receiving a response with the link template
var userUri = endpoint.LinkTemplate("user", new { id = "123" });
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

// With query parameters
var searchUri = endpoint.LinkTemplate("search", new { q = "test", limit = 10 });
// Result: http://example.com/search?q=test&limit=10

// Using a dictionary
var variables = new Dictionary<string, object> { ["id"] = "123" };
var uri = endpoint.LinkTemplate("user", variables);

// After receiving a response with the link template
URI userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("user", Map.of("id", "123"));
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

// With query parameters
URI searchUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("search", Map.of("q", "test", "limit", 10));
// Result: http://example.com/search?q=test&limit=10

// After receiving a response with the link template
val userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("user", mapOf("id" to "123"))
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

// With query parameters
val searchUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("search", mapOf("q" to "test", "limit" to 10))
// Result: http://example.com/search?q=test&limit=10

// After receiving a response with the link template
const userUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("user", { id: "123" });
// Result: http://example.com/users/123

// With query parameters
const searchUri = endpoint.linkTemplate("search", { q: "test", limit: 10 });
// Result: http://example.com/search?q=test&limit=10

docs.title: Default link templates
docs.text:
You can register default link templates that will be used when the server doesn't provide a template for a specific relation type:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
class MyEndpoint : EndpointBase
{
    public MyEndpoint(IEndpoint referrer, string relativeUri) 
        : base(referrer, relativeUri)
    {
        // Set a default template for the "child" relation
        SetDefaultLinkTemplate("child", "./{id}");
    }
}

class MyEndpoint extends AbstractEndpoint {
    public MyEndpoint(Endpoint referrer, String relativeUri) {
        super(referrer, relativeUri);
        // Set a default template for the "child" relation
        setDefaultLinkTemplate("child", "./{id}");
    }
}

class MyEndpoint(referrer: Endpoint, relativeUri: String) : AbstractEndpoint(referrer, relativeUri) {
    init {
        // Set a default template for the "child" relation
        setDefaultLinkTemplate("child", "./{id}")
    }
}

class MyEndpoint extends Endpoint {
    constructor(referrer: Endpoint, relativeUri: string) {
        super(referrer, relativeUri);
        // Set a default template for the "child" relation
        this.setDefaultLinkTemplate("child", "./{id}");
    }
}

docs.title: Built-in defaults
docs.text: Collection and Indexer endpoints automatically set a default link template of ./{id} for the child relation. This allows you to access individual elements by ID without the server explicitly providing a link template.

docs.title: Serializers
docs.text:
Serializers control how entities are serialized when sending requests and deserialized when receiving responses.

TypedRest provides serializers for various transport formats:

Format C#/.NET Java/Kotlin TypeScript JSON Built-in Built-in Built-in XML Built-in Add-on - BSON Built-in - -

You can also create and use custom serializers.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
When creating endpoints, the serializer is automatically inherited from the parent (referrer) endpoint:

C#TypeScript 
var client = new EntryEndpoint(
    new Uri("http://example.com/"),
    serializer: new SystemTextJsonSerializer());

var contacts = new CollectionEndpoint<Contact>(client, relativeUri: "./contacts");
// contacts uses the same SystemTextJsonSerializer

const client = new EntryEndpoint(
    new URL("http://example.com/"),
    new CustomSerializer());

const contacts = new CollectionEndpoint<Contact>(client, "./contacts");
// contacts.serializer is automatically set to the same CustomSerializer

This inheritance ensures consistent serialization behavior across your entire endpoint hierarchy.

docs.title: BSON
docs.text:
BSON (Binary JSON) serialization is available in the .NET implementation of TypedRest.

C#

The BSON serializer provides efficient binary serialization using Newtonsoft.Json's BSON support:

var endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    new Uri("http://example.com/"),
    serializer: new BsonSerializer());

The BSON serializer uses the same Newtonsoft.Json settings as the default JSON serializer:

  • Camel-case property naming
  • String enums with camel-case naming
  • Null values are not serialized
  • Automatic type name handling

docs.title: Content type
docs.text: The serializer handles the application/bson content type.

docs.title: Custom serializers
docs.text: If none of the built-in serializers fits your needs, you can implement your own.

docs.title: Implement the interface
docs.text:
Implement the platform's Serializer interface (or appropriate base type):

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

TypedRest uses MediaTypeFormatter from the System.Net.Http.Formatting family. Derive from MediaTypeFormatter (or one of its specializations) and override the read/write methods.

using System.Net.Http.Formatting;

public class MySerializer : MediaTypeFormatter
{
    public MySerializer()
    {
        SupportedMediaTypes.Add(new("application/my-format"));
    }

    public override bool CanReadType(Type type) => true;
    public override bool CanWriteType(Type type) => true;

    // Override ReadFromStreamAsync and WriteToStreamAsync to implement
    // custom (de)serialization logic.
}

Implement the net.typedrest.serializers.Serializer interface, or derive from AbstractJsonSerializer/AbstractXmlSerializer for JSON-/XML-based formats:

import net.typedrest.serializers.Serializer;
import okhttp3.MediaType;
import okhttp3.RequestBody;
import okhttp3.ResponseBody;
import java.util.List;

public class MySerializer implements Serializer {
    private static final MediaType MEDIA_TYPE = MediaType.get("application/my-format");

    @Override
    public List<MediaType> getSupportedMediaTypes() {
        return List.of(MEDIA_TYPE);
    }

    @Override
    public <T> RequestBody serialize(T entity, Class<T> type) {
        // Custom serialization logic
        return RequestBody.create(toBytes(entity), MEDIA_TYPE);
    }

    @Override
    public <T> RequestBody serializeList(Iterable<T> entities, Class<T> type) {
        // Custom serialization logic
        return RequestBody.create(toBytes(entities), MEDIA_TYPE);
    }

    @Override
    public <T> T deserialize(ResponseBody body, Class<T> type) {
        // Custom deserialization logic
        return fromBytes(body.bytes(), type);
    }

    @Override
    public <T> List<T> deserializeList(ResponseBody body, Class<T> type) {
        // Custom deserialization logic
        return fromBytesAsList(body.bytes(), type);
    }
}

Implement the net.typedrest.serializers.Serializer interface, or derive from AbstractJsonSerializer/AbstractXmlSerializer for JSON-/XML-based formats:

import net.typedrest.serializers.Serializer
import okhttp3.MediaType
import okhttp3.MediaType.Companion.toMediaType
import okhttp3.RequestBody
import okhttp3.RequestBody.Companion.toRequestBody
import okhttp3.ResponseBody

class MySerializer : Serializer {
    private val mediaType = "application/my-format".toMediaType()

    override val supportedMediaTypes: List<MediaType> = listOf(mediaType)

    override fun <T> serialize(entity: T, type: Class<T>): RequestBody =
        toBytes(entity).toRequestBody(mediaType)

    override fun <T> serializeList(entities: Iterable<T>, type: Class<T>): RequestBody =
        toBytes(entities).toRequestBody(mediaType)

    override fun <T> deserialize(body: ResponseBody, type: Class<T>): T? =
        fromBytes(body.bytes(), type)

    override fun <T> deserializeList(body: ResponseBody, type: Class<T>): List<T>? =
        fromBytesAsList(body.bytes(), type)
}

Implement the Serializer interface:

import { Serializer } from "typedrest/serializers";

class MySerializer implements Serializer {
    readonly supportedMediaTypes = ["application/my-format"];

    serialize<T>(entity: T): string {
        // Custom serialization logic
        return JSON.stringify(entity);
    }

    deserialize<T>(text: string): T {
        // Custom deserialization logic
        return JSON.parse(text) as T;
    }
}

docs.title: Content negotiation
docs.text:
The supportedMediaTypes property lists the MIME types this serializer can handle. TypedRest uses this information to:

  • Set the Content-Type header when sending requests.
  • Set the Accept header when receiving responses.
  • Pick the right serializer for a response based on its Content-Type header (when multiple serializers are configured).

The first entry in the list is used as the default for outgoing requests.

docs.title: Register the serializer
docs.text:
Pass an instance of your serializer to the entry endpoint constructor:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    new Uri("http://example.com/"),
    serializer: new MySerializer());

EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    (HttpCredentials) null,
    new MySerializer());

val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = MySerializer())

const endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    new URL("http://example.com/"),
    new MySerializer());

All child endpoints created from this entry endpoint automatically inherit the serializer.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
JSON is the default serialization format in TypedRest.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

Newtonsoft.Json (Default)

The default serializer uses Newtonsoft.Json with the following settings:

  • Camel-case property naming
  • String enums with camel-case naming
  • Null values are not serialized
  • Automatic type name handling
var endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(new Uri("http://example.com/")); // Uses NewtonsoftJsonSerializer by default

To customize the serializer settings:

var endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    new Uri("http://example.com/"),
    serializer: new NewtonsoftJsonSerializer
    {
        SerializerSettings =
        {
            DateFormatString = "yyyy-MM-dd"
        }
    });

System.Text.Json

You can also use the System.Text.Json serializer with the TypedRest.SystemTextJson NuGet package. Default settings:

  • Web defaults (camel-case property naming)
  • Null values are not serialized when writing

Basic usage:

var endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    new Uri("http://example.com/"),
    serializer: new SystemTextJsonSerializer());

To customize the serializer options:

var endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    new Uri("http://example.com/"),
    serializer: new SystemTextJsonSerializer
    {
        Options =
        {
            WriteIndented = true,
            Converters = {new JsonStringEnumConverter() }
        }
    });

kotlinx.serialization (Default)

The default serializer uses kotlinx.serialization.

EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/")); // Uses KotlinxJsonSerializer by default

Not usable with entities written in Java

kotlinx.serialization generates its serializers with a Kotlin compiler plugin, so it only works for entity classes written in Kotlin and annotated with @Serializable. A Java class has no generated serializer, and deserializing one fails at runtime rather than at compile time.

If your entities are Java classes, pick Jackson or Moshi below. Both work by reflection and handle either language.

Jackson

For Java POJOs or more control over serialization, add the typedrest-serializers-jackson dependency and pass a JacksonJsonSerializer:

EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/"), (HttpCredentials) null, new JacksonJsonSerializer());

To customize the JsonMapper:

JsonMapper mapper = JsonMapper.builder()
    .addModule(new KotlinModule.Builder().build())
    .disable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES)
    .build();
EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/"), (HttpCredentials) null, new JacksonJsonSerializer(mapper));

Moshi

Add the typedrest-serializers-moshi dependency and pass a MoshiJsonSerializer:

EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/"), (HttpCredentials) null, new MoshiJsonSerializer());

kotlinx.serialization (Default)

The default serializer uses kotlinx.serialization. Annotate entity classes with @Serializable:

import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

@Serializable
data class Contact(val name: String)

val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/")) // Uses KotlinxJsonSerializer by default

Jackson

Add the typedrest-serializers-jackson dependency and pass a JacksonJsonSerializer:

val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = JacksonJsonSerializer()
)

To customize the JsonMapper:

val mapper = JsonMapper.builder()
    .addModule(kotlinModule())
    .disable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES)
    .build()
val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = JacksonJsonSerializer(mapper)
)

Moshi

Add the typedrest-serializers-moshi dependency and pass a MoshiJsonSerializer:

val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = MoshiJsonSerializer()
)

To customize the Moshi instance:

val moshi = Moshi.Builder()
    .add(KotlinJsonAdapterFactory())
    .add(Date::class.java, Rfc3339DateJsonAdapter())
    .build()
val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = MoshiJsonSerializer(moshi)
)

Native JSON (Default)

The default serializer uses the native JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse() methods.

const endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(new URL("http://example.com/")); // Uses JsonSerializer by default

docs.title: Content type
docs.text: The serializer handles the application/json content type. TypedRest also automatically treats custom media types ending in +json (e.g., application/vnd.api+json, application/hal+json) as JSON and deserializes them using the configured JSON serializer.

docs.title: XML
docs.text:
XML serialization is available in the .NET and Java/Kotlin implementations of TypedRest.

C#JavaKotlin

The XML serializer uses .NET's built-in System.Xml.Serialization.XmlSerializer:

var endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(
    new Uri("http://example.com/"),
    serializer: new XmlSerializer());

Jackson XML

Add the typedrest-serializers-jackson-xml dependency and pass a JacksonXmlSerializer:

EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/"), (HttpCredentials) null, new JacksonXmlSerializer());

To customize the XmlMapper:

XmlMapper mapper = XmlMapper.builder()
    .addModule(new KotlinModule.Builder().build())
    .disable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES)
    .build();
EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/"), (HttpCredentials) null, new JacksonXmlSerializer(mapper));

XmlUtil

Add the typedrest-serializers-xmlutil dependency and pass an XmlUtilSerializer:

EntryEndpoint endpoint = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("http://example.com/"), (HttpCredentials) null, new XmlUtilSerializer());

Not usable with entities written in Java

XmlUtil builds on kotlinx.serialization, which generates its serializers with a Kotlin compiler plugin. It only works for entity classes written in Kotlin and annotated with @Serializable. A Java class has no generated serializer, and deserializing one fails at runtime rather than at compile time.

If your entities are Java classes, use Jackson XML above instead.

Jackson XML

Add the typedrest-serializers-jackson-xml dependency and pass a JacksonXmlSerializer:

val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = JacksonXmlSerializer()
)

To customize the XmlMapper:

val mapper = XmlMapper.builder()
    .addModule(kotlinModule())
    .disable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES)
    .build()
val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = JacksonXmlSerializer(mapper)
)

XmlUtil

Add the typedrest-serializers-xmlutil dependency and annotate entity classes with @Serializable:

import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

@Serializable
data class Contact(val name: String)

val endpoint = EntryEndpoint(
    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = XmlUtilSerializer()
)

To customize the XML instance:

    indentString = "  "
}

    URI.create("http://example.com/"),
    serializer = XmlUtilSerializer(xml)

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
If you wish to use TypedRest in an ASP.NET Core web service (or any other kind of application that uses IServiceCollection-based dependency injection) you can use the .AddTypedRest() extension method. It registers your entry endpoint as a typed HTTP client, so its HttpClient is created and configured by IHttpClientFactory:

// Register the client class itself
services.AddTypedRest<MyClient>(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"));

// Register the client class behind an interface
services.AddTypedRest<IMyClient, MyClient>(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"));

The client class must have a constructor that takes an HttpClient. AddTypedRest() sets the HttpClient's BaseAddress to the URI you pass, which the entry endpoint then uses as its own URI:

class MyClient : EntryEndpoint, IMyClient
{
    public MyClient(Uri uri) : base(uri) {} // For use without dependency injection

    public MyClient(HttpClient httpClient) : base(httpClient) {} // For AddTypedRest()

    // ...
}

Typed clients are registered as transient, and IHttpClientFactory recycles the underlying connections periodically so that DNS changes are picked up. Do not keep a client in a singleton for the lifetime of the application, as that bypasses this recycling. If a singleton needs the client, inject IServiceScopeFactory or IHttpClientFactory and create a client when needed.

AddTypedRest() returns an IHttpClientBuilder, so all of the usual HTTP client configuration (timeouts, message handlers, resilience) is available. TypedRest adds two authentication methods on top:

.AddBasicAuth() Sends HTTP Basic credentials. Takes either a delegate that fills in a NetworkCredential, e.g. from configuration, or an ICredentials provider that is queried for the client's URI. .AddOAuthHandler() Adds the OAuth handler from TypedRest.OAuth. Takes a delegate that configures OAuthOptions, a delegate that builds them from the IServiceProvider, or the identity server URI, client ID and client secret directly. Options are created separately for each client, so several clients in one application can authenticate against different identity servers. Options set with a configuring delegate or passed directly are registered as named options under the name of the client's HttpClient. 
services.AddTypedRest<IMyClient, MyClient>(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"))
    .AddOAuthHandler(options => configuration.GetSection("MyClient:OAuth").Bind(options));

docs.title: OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
The TypedRest.OAuth package provides OAuthHandler, an HttpClient message handler that authenticates requests using the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow, the usual flow for service-to-service calls. It does not depend on the rest of TypedRest, so you can use it with any HttpClient.

var handler = new OAuthHandler(
    new OAuthOptions
    {
        Uri = new Uri("https://identity.example.com/"),
        ClientId = "my-client",
        ClientSecret = clientSecret,
        Scope = "my-scope"
    },
    innerHandler: new HttpClientHandler());

var client = new MyClient(new HttpClient(handler) { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://example.com/api/") });
Option Description Default Uri (required) The identity server to request tokens from ClientId (required) The client identifier to present to the identity server ClientSecret (required) The client secret to present to the identity server Scope The scope to request a token for Audience The audience to request a token for TokenLifetimeBuffer How long before a token expires to request a new one 1 minute

On the first request, the handler finds the token endpoint using OpenID Connect discovery on Uri, requests a token and sends it as a Bearer header. It reuses the token until TokenLifetimeBuffer before it expires.

If the server still responds with 401 Unauthorized, and its WWW-Authenticate header reports error="invalid_token" or gives no details, the handler requests a new token and retries the request once. Requests with streamed content, such as uploads, are not retried, because their body cannot be sent a second time.

With dependency injection, use .AddOAuthHandler() instead of building the handler yourself.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
A TypedRest client sits between your application and an API, so there are three things worth testing:

Testing endpoints Verify that your TypedRest endpoint wrappers issue the correct HTTP requests, correctly parse responses and turn error responses into the right exceptions. Uses a mock HTTP server to intercept calls at the network layer. Catches wrong URIs, methods, bodies or error handling. Mocking endpoints Test service or business logic that depends on TypedRest endpoints without making any HTTP calls. TypedRest endpoints implement interfaces, so they integrate naturally with standard mocking frameworks. Catches bugs in your own logic. Integration testing Run the service in the test process and point the client at it. Catches mismatches between client and service, such as differing routes, unexpected status codes or properties serialized differently.

The Testing your client tutorial applies all three to one client.

docs.title: Testing endpoints
docs.text:
To verify that your TypedRest endpoint configuration issues the correct HTTP requests and correctly deserializes responses, use a mock HTTP server. This lets you write fast, deterministic tests without a running API server.

Most of what an endpoint does comes from TypedRest and is tested there. What is specific to your client is its structure: does each child endpoint point to the right URI and use the right endpoint type? One test per child endpoint is usually enough. You don't need to test every method of every endpoint.

docs.title: Verifying requests
Testing error responses
docs.text:
A mock server is also the easiest way to produce error responses that are hard to cause with a real API. Respond with an error status and check that TypedRest maps it to the expected exception:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
mock.Expect(HttpMethod.Get, "http://localhost/contacts/1")
    .Respond(HttpStatusCode.NotFound);

await Assert.ThrowsAsync<KeyNotFoundException>(() => endpoint.ReadAsync());

server.enqueue(new MockResponse().setResponseCode(404));

assertThrows(NotFoundException.class, endpoint::read);

server.enqueue(MockResponse().setResponseCode(404))

assertThrows<NotFoundException> { endpoint.read() }

import { NotFoundError } from 'typedrest/errors';

test('contact not found', async () => {
    fetchMock.mockOnceIf('http://localhost/contacts/1', '', { status: 404 });

    await expect(endpoint.read()).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(NotFoundError);
});

The same approach tests how your application reacts to 401, 403 or 500 responses, or to a 412 Precondition Failed after a write with an outdated ETag (see Optimistic concurrency).

docs.title: Integration testing
docs.text:
If you write the service as well as the client, test the two together. This catches the mistakes neither endpoint tests nor mocks can: a route that differs between client and service, a status code the client does not expect, or a property the two serialize differently.

Run the service inside the test process and point the client at it. Replace the service's own dependencies, such as its database, with mocks, so the test only covers the HTTP layer.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

Use WebApplicationFactory from Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing, which hosts the service in memory and provides an HttpClient connected to it. Give your client a constructor that passes an HttpClient on to the entry endpoint:

public class MyClient : EntryEndpoint
{
    public MyClient(Uri uri) : base(uri) {}

    public MyClient(HttpClient httpClient) : base(httpClient) {}

    // Child endpoints
}

The entry endpoint then uses the HttpClient's BaseAddress as its URI:

public class ContactsApiFacts(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory) : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly Mock<IContactsService> _service = new();

    private MyClient CreateClient()
        => new(factory
            .WithWebHostBuilder(x => x.ConfigureTestServices(services => services.AddSingleton(_service.Object)))
            .CreateClient());

    [Fact]
    public async Task ReadsContact()
    {
        _service.Setup(x => x.ReadAsync("1337")).ReturnsAsync(new Contact { Id = "1337", Name = "Smith" });

        var contact = await CreateClient().Contacts["1337"].ReadAsync();

        Assert.Equal("Smith", contact.Name);
    }
}

IContactsService stands for whatever the service's controllers depend on. If the service uses top-level statements, add public partial class Program; to it so the test can reference Program.

Sample-DotNet has a complete set of tests like this, using TestServer directly.

Use @SpringBootTest to start the service on a random port, and @MockitoBean to replace its dependencies:

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class ContactsApiTest {
    @LocalServerPort
    private int port;

    @MockitoBean
    private ContactsService service;

    @Test
    void readsContact() {
        Contact smith = new Contact("Smith");
        smith.setId("1337");
        when(service.read("1337")).thenReturn(smith);
        MyClient client = new MyClient(URI.create("http://localhost:" + port + "/"));

        Contact contact = client.getContacts().get("1337").read();

        assertEquals("Smith", contact.getName());
    }
}

ContactsService stands for whatever the service's controllers depend on.

Use @SpringBootTest to start the service on a random port, and @MockitoBean to replace its dependencies:

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class ContactsApiTest {
    @LocalServerPort
    private var port: Int = 0

    @MockitoBean
    private lateinit var service: ContactsService

    @Test
    fun readsContact() {
        whenever(service.read("1337")).thenReturn(Contact(id = "1337", name = "Smith"))
        val client = MyClient(URI("http://localhost:$port/"))

        val contact = client.contacts["1337"].read()

        assertEquals("Smith", contact.name)
    }
}

ContactsService stands for whatever the service's controllers depend on. Sample-Kotlin has a complete set of tests like this.

If the service is written in another language, test the TypeScript client against a running instance of it, for example one started in your CI pipeline, or rely on endpoint tests with a mock server.

Sharing the entity classes between client and service, as the sample projects do with a separate DTO project, rules out a whole class of mismatches before any test runs.

docs.title: Mocking endpoints
docs.text: TypedRest endpoint classes implement interfaces, making them straightforward to mock with standard testing frameworks. This allows you to test service or business logic that depends on TypedRest endpoints without making any HTTP calls.

docs.title: Example service
docs.text:
Consider a service that filters contacts via a TypedRest endpoint:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
class ContactService(ICollectionEndpoint<Contact> contacts)
{
    public async Task<List<Contact>> GetActiveContactsAsync(CancellationToken ct = default)
        => (await contacts.ReadAllAsync(ct))
            .Where(c => c.IsActive)
            .ToList();
}

class ContactService {
    private final CollectionEndpoint<Contact> contacts;

    ContactService(CollectionEndpoint<Contact> contacts) {
        this.contacts = contacts;
    }

    List<Contact> getActiveContacts() {
        return contacts.readAll().stream()
            .filter(Contact::isActive)
            .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

class ContactService(private val contacts: CollectionEndpoint<Contact>) {
    fun getActiveContacts(): List<Contact> =
        contacts.readAll().filter { it.isActive }
}

class ContactService {
    constructor(private contacts: CollectionEndpoint<Contact>) {}

    async getActiveContacts(): Promise<Contact[]> {
        return (await this.contacts.readAll()).filter(c => c.isActive);
    }
}

docs.title: Unit tests with mocks
Mocking a custom client
docs.text:
Real clients are trees of endpoints: an entry endpoint with child endpoints, some of them custom endpoint types with children of their own. To mock code that navigates such a tree, for example by calling Contacts["1337"].Poke, each level of the chain needs to be mockable. The examples below test a WelcomeService that pokes the contact with a given ID.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

Mocking libraries such as Moq can only intercept interface members and virtual methods. TypedRest's own endpoints all have interfaces; give your custom endpoints interfaces too, and use the interfaces in your client's properties:

public interface IContactEndpoint : IElementEndpoint<Contact>
{
    IElementEndpoint<Note> Note { get; }
    IActionEndpoint Poke { get; }
}

public class ContactEndpoint(IEndpoint referrer, Uri relativeUri)
    : ElementEndpoint<Contact>(referrer, relativeUri), IContactEndpoint
{
    public IElementEndpoint<Note> Note => new ElementEndpoint<Note>(this, relativeUri: "./note");
    public IActionEndpoint Poke => new ActionEndpoint(this, relativeUri: "./poke");
}

public interface IMyClient : IEndpoint
{
    ICollectionEndpoint<Contact, IContactEndpoint> Contacts { get; }
}

public class MyClient(Uri uri) : EntryEndpoint(uri), IMyClient
{
    public ICollectionEndpoint<Contact, IContactEndpoint> Contacts
        => new CollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint>(this, relativeUri: "./contacts");
}

ICollectionEndpoint is covariant in the element endpoint type, so a collection of ContactEndpoints can be exposed as a collection of IContactEndpoints. The code generator can create interfaces like these for you.

Moq can then set up and verify the whole chain in one expression:

var client = new Mock<IMyClient>();
client.Setup(x => x.Contacts["1337"].Poke.InvokeAsync(It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()))
      .Returns(Task.CompletedTask);

await new WelcomeService(client.Object).WelcomeAsync("1337");

client.Verify(x => x.Contacts["1337"].Poke.InvokeAsync(It.IsAny<CancellationToken>()));

Mockito can mock classes as well as interfaces, so custom endpoints don't need interfaces of their own. Stub each level of the chain, here for a client whose getContacts() returns a GenericCollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint>:

ActionEndpoint poke = mock(ActionEndpoint.class);
ContactEndpoint contact = mock(ContactEndpoint.class);
when(contact.getPoke()).thenReturn(poke);
GenericCollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint> contacts = mock(GenericCollectionEndpoint.class);
when(contacts.get("1337")).thenReturn(contact);
MyClient client = mock(MyClient.class);
when(client.getContacts()).thenReturn(contacts);

new WelcomeService(client).welcome("1337");

verify(poke).invoke();

mockito-kotlin can mock classes as well as interfaces, so custom endpoints don't need interfaces of their own. Kotlin classes are final by default, which Mockito 5 handles out of the box. Stub each level of the chain, here for a client whose contacts is a GenericCollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint>:

val poke = mock<ActionEndpoint>()
val contact = mock<ContactEndpoint> { on { this.poke } doReturn poke }
val contacts = mock<GenericCollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint>> { on { get("1337") } doReturn contact }
val client = mock<MyClient> { on { this.contacts } doReturn contacts }

WelcomeService(client).welcome("1337")

verify(poke).invoke()

Build a plain object for each level of the chain, with only the members your code uses:

const poke = { invoke: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined) };
const contacts = { get: jest.fn().mockReturnValue({ poke }) };
const client = { contacts } as unknown as MyClient;

await new WelcomeService(client).welcome('1337');

expect(contacts.get).toHaveBeenCalledWith('1337');
expect(poke.invoke).toHaveBeenCalled();
