docs.text: The other sections of this site describe each part of TypedRest on its own. The tutorials here combine those parts to complete a whole task, from an empty project to working code.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Pick one of these depending on whether your API has an OpenAPI document:

Build your first client Write a client by hand, one endpoint at a time, and learn how TypedRest models an API along the way. Generate a client from OpenAPI Let the code generator build the client, check what it inferred and fix what it got wrong.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text: Authentication Send credentials, API keys and OAuth 2.0 tokens, and handle authentication errors. Dependency injection Register a client in ASP.NET Core and configure its HTTP client. Command-line tool Turn a .NET client into a command-line interface. Optimistic concurrency Use ETags to keep two clients from overwriting each other's changes. Paging Read large collections in pages using HTTP range requests. Live updates Get notified of changes by polling, streaming or Server-Sent Events, and choose between them. Testing your client Test endpoints, the code that uses them, and client and service together.

docs.title: The example API
docs.text:
All tutorials use the address book API from the Introduction:

Path Methods Description /contacts GET, POST All contacts. POST adds one and returns its URI in the Location header. /contacts/{id} GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE A single contact. /contacts/{id}/note GET, PUT A note attached to a contact. /contacts/{id}/poke POST Pokes a contact. Takes no input and returns no output.

The tutorials share these entity classes:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
public class Contact
{
    public string? Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; } = "";
    public string? Email { get; set; }
}

public class Note
{
    public string Content { get; set; } = "";
}

public class Contact {
    private String id;
    private String name;
    private String email;

    public Contact() {}

    public Contact(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    // Getters and setters omitted
}

public class Note {
    private String content;

    public Note() {}

    public Note(String content) {
        this.content = content;
    }

    // Getter and setter omitted
}

These are plain Java classes, so they need a reflection-based serializer such as Jackson. The tutorials pass a JacksonJsonSerializer wherever an entry endpoint is created.

@Serializable
data class Contact(val id: String? = null, val name: String, val email: String? = null)

@Serializable
data class Note(val content: String)

interface Contact {
    id?: string;
    name: string;
    email?: string;
}

interface Note {
    content: string;
}

The Sample-DotNet and Sample-Kotlin projects implement the same API as a working service and client, if you want to run the examples against a real server.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Every endpoint in a client sends its requests through the HTTP client of the entry endpoint. Authentication therefore goes in one place: configure the entry endpoint or its HTTP client, and every request from the client is authenticated.

This tutorial extends the AddressBookClient from Build your first client with each common scheme, from the simplest to the most involved.

docs.title: HTTP Basic authentication
docs.text:
Pass a username and password when creating the entry endpoint:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
public class AddressBookClient(Uri uri, NetworkCredential? credentials = null)
    : EntryEndpoint(uri, credentials)
{
    // ...
}

var client = new AddressBookClient(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"), new NetworkCredential("alice", "secret"));

public class AddressBookClient extends EntryEndpoint {
    public AddressBookClient(URI uri, HttpCredentials credentials) {
        super(uri, credentials, new JacksonJsonSerializer());
    }

    // ...
}

AddressBookClient client = new AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"), new HttpCredentials("alice", "secret"));

class AddressBookClient(uri: URI, credentials: HttpCredentials? = null) : EntryEndpoint(uri, credentials) {
    // ...
}

val client = AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"), HttpCredentials("alice", "secret"))

The TypeScript entry endpoint has no credentials parameter. Set the header on its HTTP client instead:

const client = new AddressBookClient(new URL("https://example.com/api/"));
client.httpClient.defaultHeaders.set("Authorization", `Basic ${btoa("alice:secret")}`);

In .NET, Java and Kotlin you can also put the credentials in the URI.

docs.title: API keys and static bearer tokens
docs.text:
Many APIs take a fixed key or token in a header. Add the header to the HTTP client once:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var client = new AddressBookClient(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"));
client.HttpClient.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new("Bearer", token);

// or, for a custom header:
client.HttpClient.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("X-Api-Key", apiKey);

TypedRest for the JVM uses OkHttp. Add an interceptor that sets the header, and pass the configured OkHttpClient to the entry endpoint:

public class AddressBookClient extends EntryEndpoint {
    public AddressBookClient(URI uri, OkHttpClient httpClient) {
        super(uri, httpClient, new JacksonJsonSerializer());
    }

    // ...
}

OkHttpClient httpClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(chain -> chain.proceed(chain.request().newBuilder()
        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
        .build()))
    .build();
AddressBookClient client = new AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"), httpClient);

TypedRest for the JVM uses OkHttp. Add an interceptor that sets the header, and pass the configured OkHttpClient to the entry endpoint:

class AddressBookClient(uri: URI, httpClient: OkHttpClient) : EntryEndpoint(uri, httpClient) {
    // ...
}

val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor { chain ->
        chain.proceed(chain.request().newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer $token")
            .build())
    }
    .build()
val client = AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"), httpClient)

const client = new AddressBookClient(new URL("https://example.com/api/"));
client.httpClient.defaultHeaders.set("Authorization", `Bearer ${token}`);

// or, for a custom header:
client.httpClient.defaultHeaders.set("X-Api-Key", apiKey);

Child endpoints share the entry endpoint's HTTP client, so this covers every request the client makes.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 tokens that expire
docs.text:
Tokens from an OAuth 2.0 identity server expire, so a fixed header is not enough. The client has to request a token, reuse it while it is valid, and request a new one before or when it expires.

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

The TypedRest.OAuth package does all of this for the client credentials flow, the usual flow for service-to-service calls:

dotnet add package TypedRest.OAuth

Give the client a constructor that takes an HttpClient, and build that HttpClient with an OAuthHandler:

public class AddressBookClient : EntryEndpoint
{
    public AddressBookClient(Uri uri) : base(uri) {}

    public AddressBookClient(HttpClient httpClient) : base(httpClient) {}

    // ...
}

var handler = new OAuthHandler(
    new OAuthOptions
    {
        Uri = new Uri("https://identity.example.com/"),
        ClientId = "address-book-sync",
        ClientSecret = clientSecret,
        Scope = "contacts"
    },
    innerHandler: new HttpClientHandler());

var client = new AddressBookClient(new HttpClient(handler) { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://example.com/api/") });

The handler finds the token endpoint on the identity server, reuses each token until shortly before it expires, and retries once with a new token if the server rejects one. OAuth 2.0 describes this in detail and lists all options.

In ASP.NET Core and other applications that use IServiceCollection, call .AddOAuthHandler() instead of building the handler yourself; see Dependency injection.

TypedRest for the JVM has no built-in OAuth support. An OkHttp interceptor of your own can cache the token and refresh it on a 401 Unauthorized:

public record AccessToken(String value, Instant expiresAt) {}

public class OAuthInterceptor implements Interceptor {
    private final Supplier<AccessToken> tokenSource;
    private AccessToken token;

    public OAuthInterceptor(Supplier<AccessToken> tokenSource) {
        this.tokenSource = tokenSource;
    }

    private synchronized String getToken(boolean refresh) {
        if (refresh || token == null || Instant.now().isAfter(token.expiresAt().minusSeconds(60))) {
            token = tokenSource.get();
        }
        return token.value();
    }

    @Override
    public Response intercept(Chain chain) throws IOException {
        Response response = chain.proceed(withBearer(chain.request(), getToken(false)));
        if (response.code() != 401) return response;

        response.close();
        return chain.proceed(withBearer(chain.request(), getToken(true)));
    }

    private static Request withBearer(Request request, String token) {
        return request.newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token).build();
    }
}

OkHttpClient httpClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(new OAuthInterceptor(() -> requestTokenFromIdentityServer()))
    .build();
AddressBookClient client = new AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"), httpClient);

requestTokenFromIdentityServer() stands for whatever obtains a token in your setup, such as a call to your identity server's token endpoint or an OAuth library like Nimbus.

TypedRest for the JVM has no built-in OAuth support. An OkHttp interceptor of your own can cache the token and refresh it on a 401 Unauthorized:

data class AccessToken(val value: String, val expiresAt: Instant)

class OAuthInterceptor(private val tokenSource: () -> AccessToken) : Interceptor {
    private var token: AccessToken? = null

    @Synchronized
    private fun getToken(refresh: Boolean): String {
        val current = token
        if (!refresh && current != null && Instant.now() < current.expiresAt.minusSeconds(60)) return current.value
        return tokenSource().also { token = it }.value
    }

    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val response = chain.proceed(chain.request().withBearer(getToken(refresh = false)))
        if (response.code != 401) return response

        response.close()
        return chain.proceed(chain.request().withBearer(getToken(refresh = true)))
    }

    private fun Request.withBearer(token: String) =
        newBuilder().header("Authorization", "Bearer $token").build()
}

val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(OAuthInterceptor { requestTokenFromIdentityServer() })
    .build()
val client = AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"), httpClient)

requestTokenFromIdentityServer() stands for whatever obtains a token in your setup, such as a call to your identity server's token endpoint or an OAuth library like Nimbus.

TypedRest for TypeScript has no built-in OAuth support. Derive from FetchHttpClient to add the token to each request and refresh it on a 401 Unauthorized:

import { FetchHttpClient, HttpMethod } from "typedrest/http";

interface AccessToken {
    value: string;
    expiresAt: number; // milliseconds since the epoch
}

export class OAuthHttpClient extends FetchHttpClient {
    private token?: AccessToken;

    constructor(private readonly tokenSource: () => Promise<AccessToken>) {
        super();
    }

    async send(uri: URL, method: HttpMethod, signal?: AbortSignal, headers?: HeadersInit, body?: BodyInit) {
        const response = await super.send(uri, method, signal, await this.withBearer(headers), body);
        if (response.status !== 401) return response;

        this.token = undefined;
        return super.send(uri, method, signal, await this.withBearer(headers), body);
    }

    private async withBearer(headers?: HeadersInit) {
        if (!this.token || Date.now() >= this.token.expiresAt - 60_000) {
            this.token = await this.tokenSource();
        }
        const result = new Headers(headers);
        result.set("Authorization", `Bearer ${this.token.value}`);
        return result;
    }
}

// The HTTP client is the fifth argument of the entry endpoint constructor
const client = new AddressBookClient(
    new URL("https://example.com/api/"), undefined, undefined, undefined,
    new OAuthHttpClient(() => requestTokenFromIdentityServer()));

requestTokenFromIdentityServer() stands for whatever obtains a token in your setup. In a browser, that is usually the library handling the user's login, such as oidc-client-ts.

Retrying requests with streamed bodies

The retry after a 401 sends the request body a second time. That is fine for the serialized entities TypedRest sends, but a body that can only be read once, such as a stream passed to an upload endpoint, cannot be replayed. The .NET OAuthHandler skips the retry for such requests; do the same if your own implementation handles uploads.

docs.title: Handling authentication errors
docs.text:
When the server rejects the credentials or the caller lacks permissions, TypedRest throws an exception you can catch:

Status Meaning .NET Java/Kotlin TypeScript 401 Unauthorized missing or invalid credentials AuthenticationException AuthenticationException AuthenticationError 403 Forbidden valid credentials, no permission UnauthorizedAccessException AuthorizationException AuthorizationError C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
try
{
    await client.Contacts["1337"].DeleteAsync();
}
catch (AuthenticationException)
{
    // Ask the user to log in again
}
catch (UnauthorizedAccessException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("You are not allowed to delete contacts.");
}

try {
    client.getContacts().get("1337").delete();
} catch (AuthenticationException ex) {
    // Ask the user to log in again
} catch (AuthorizationException ex) {
    System.out.println("You are not allowed to delete contacts.");
}

try {
    client.contacts["1337"].delete()
} catch (ex: AuthenticationException) {
    // Ask the user to log in again
} catch (ex: AuthorizationException) {
    println("You are not allowed to delete contacts.")
}

import { AuthenticationError, AuthorizationError } from "typedrest/errors";

try {
    await client.contacts.get("1337").delete();
} catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof AuthenticationError) {
        // Ask the user to log in again
    } else if (err instanceof AuthorizationError) {
        console.log("You are not allowed to delete contacts.");
    } else {
        throw err;
    }
}

Instead of handling 403 after the fact, you can often ask first. Endpoints record the Allow header of each response, so after reading a contact you can check on the same endpoint object whether deleting is allowed (DeleteAllowed in .NET, isDeleteAllowed in Java/Kotlin, deleteAllowed in TypeScript) and hide the delete button if it is not.

docs.title: Command-line tool
docs.text:
Note

This tutorial is .NET only. TypedRest.CommandLine has no Java or TypeScript equivalent.

A TypedRest client already describes the structure of an API: which resources exist, how they nest, and what can be done with each. TypedRest.CommandLine uses that to build a command-line interface with very little extra code. Each argument navigates one level deeper into the client, and the last one picks the operation:

addressbook contacts                           →  GET    /contacts
addressbook contacts create '{"name":"Smith"}' →  POST   /contacts
addressbook contacts 1337                      →  GET    /contacts/1337
addressbook contacts 1337 note                 →  GET    /contacts/1337/note
addressbook contacts 1337 poke                 →  POST   /contacts/1337/poke
addressbook contacts 1337 delete               →  DELETE /contacts/1337

This tutorial builds that tool for the AddressBookClient from Build your first client.

docs.title: 1. Create the project
docs.text:
dotnet new console -n AddressBook.Cli
cd AddressBook.Cli
dotnet add package TypedRest.CommandLine

Then add a reference to the project or package that contains your client, or copy the client classes into the new project.

docs.title: 2. Mirror the client with commands
docs.text:
For each endpoint type there is a command type in the TypedRest.CommandLine.Commands namespace that maps arguments onto that endpoint's methods: CollectionCommand for collection endpoints, ElementCommand for element endpoints, ActionCommand for action endpoints, and so on.

Start with the root command. It derives from EntryCommand and names the top-level commands:

using TypedRest.CommandLine.Commands;
using TypedRest.CommandLine.Commands.Generic;

class AddressBookCommand : EntryCommand<AddressBookClient>
{
    public AddressBookCommand(AddressBookClient client)
        : base(client)
    {
        Add("contacts", x => new CollectionCommand<Contact, ContactEndpoint, ContactCommand>(x.Contacts));
    }
}

CollectionCommand takes three type arguments here: the entity, the element endpoint type the collection hands out, and the command to use for those elements. A plain ElementCommand<Contact> would only offer reading, setting, merging and deleting a contact. To reach the note and the poke action, write a command for ContactEndpoint that adds them as sub-commands:

using TypedRest.CommandLine.Commands.Rpc;

class ContactCommand : ElementCommand<Contact>
{
    private readonly ContactEndpoint _contact;

    public ContactCommand(ContactEndpoint endpoint)
        : base(endpoint)
    {
        _contact = endpoint;
    }

    protected override IEndpointCommand? GetSubCommand(string name)
        => name.ToLowerInvariant() switch
        {
            "note" => new ElementCommand<Note>(_contact.Note),
            "poke" => new ActionCommand(_contact.Poke),
            _ => base.GetSubCommand(name)
        };
}

The collection command creates ContactCommands through their constructor, so it must be public and take exactly one ContactEndpoint.

docs.title: 3. Run the commands
docs.text:
An Executor connects everything. It builds the client, creates the root command, passes it the arguments and turns exceptions into error messages and exit codes. Replace the contents of Program.cs:

using TypedRest.CommandLine;

return await new Executor<AddressBookClient, AddressBookCommand>().RunAsync(args);

By default, the Executor creates the client by calling its constructor that takes a Uri. The first time you run the tool, it asks for the API's URI and an OAuth token, and stores both in a folder named after your executable in the user's application data directory. Later runs reuse them. If the API answers with 401 Unauthorized, the stored token is deleted and the tool asks for a new one.

If the API has a link with the relation type token-provider, the tool opens that page in the browser when it asks for a token, so users can log in and copy a token from there.

Providing the URI without prompting

A file named uri next to the executable takes precedence over the stored URI. Ship one with the tool to point it at a fixed server.

docs.title: 4. Use your own way of building the client
docs.text:
The default behavior suits APIs that use bearer tokens. For anything else, implement IEndpointProvider and pass it to the Executor. This one reads the URI from an environment variable and uses no authentication:

class AddressBookProvider : IEndpointProvider<AddressBookClient>
{
    public AddressBookClient Build()
        => new(new Uri(Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("ADDRESSBOOK_URI") ?? "http://localhost:5000/"));

    public void ResetAuthentication() {}
}

return await new Executor<AddressBookClient, AddressBookCommand>(new AddressBookProvider()).RunAsync(args);

To keep the config files and prompts but change some details, derive from EndpointProviderBase or CliEndpointProvider instead. For example, override ConfigDir to store the settings somewhere else.

docs.title: 5. Try it
docs.text:
# GET /contacts
addressbook contacts

# GET /contacts with Range: elements=0-9
addressbook contacts 0-9

# POST /contacts, then GET the new contact and print it
addressbook contacts create '{"name":"Smith","email":"smith@example.com"}'

# The same, reading the JSON from stdin
echo '{"name":"Smith"}' | addressbook contacts create

# GET /contacts/1337
addressbook contacts 1337

# PUT /contacts/1337
addressbook contacts 1337 set '{"id":"1337","name":"Smith","email":"j.smith@example.com"}'

# GET and PUT /contacts/1337/note
addressbook contacts 1337 note
addressbook contacts 1337 note set '{"content":"Call back on Monday"}'

# POST /contacts/1337/poke
addressbook contacts 1337 poke

# DELETE /contacts/1337
addressbook contacts 1337 delete

Running addressbook on its own lists the top-level commands.

Entities are printed as indented JSON, unless their class overrides ToString(). A collection argument containing exactly one -, such as 0-9, 10- or -5, is read as a range rather than an ID; IDs of that form cannot be addressed this way.

docs.title: 6. Use the exit codes in scripts
docs.text:
The Executor maps exceptions to exit codes, so scripts can react to specific errors:

Exit code Cause 0 Success 1 Missing or invalid arguments 2 400 Bad Request 3 403 Forbidden 4 401 Unauthorized, even after asking for a new token 5 404 Not Found or 410 Gone, or no URI or token could be obtained 6 409 Conflict, 412 Precondition Failed or 416 Range Not Satisfiable 10 Other HTTP error status 11 Invalid JSON 12 I/O error 99 Canceled 
if ! addressbook contacts 1337 > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "Contact 1337 is missing"
fi

docs.title: 7. Customize input and output
docs.text:
Override OutputEntity (or OutputEntities in collection commands) to print something other than JSON:

class ContactCommand : ElementCommand<Contact>
{
    // ...

    protected override void OutputEntity(Contact entity)
        => Console.Write($"{entity.Name} <{entity.Email}>");
}

Console here is the command's IConsole, which writes to stdout, stderr and reads from stdin. Replace it with your own implementation to change how all output is formatted. Similarly, override InputEntity to build an entity from arguments such as --name Smith instead of JSON.

For endpoint types with no matching command, or to add operations of your own, derive from EndpointCommand<TEndpoint> and override ExecuteInnerAsync.

docs.title: Optimistic concurrency
docs.text:
Two people open the same contact. Alice changes the email address and saves. A moment later Bob, still looking at the old version, fixes a typo in the name and saves too. Bob's request replaces the whole contact, so Alice's new email address is silently lost.

HTTP solves this "lost update" problem with entity tags (ETags), and TypedRest uses them automatically if the server provides them. This tutorial shows what TypedRest does, how to handle conflicts, and what the server needs to do.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. When an element endpoint reads an entity, the server includes an ETag header identifying that version of it, such as "v7". The endpoint keeps the response along with the ETag.
  2. When the same endpoint later sets (PUT) or deletes the entity, it sends If-Match: "v7", meaning "only do this if the entity is still at version v7".
  3. If someone else changed the entity in the meantime, the server answers 412 Precondition Failed instead of applying the change, and TypedRest throws an exception.

The same ETag also saves bandwidth: reading the entity again with the same endpoint sends If-None-Match: "v7", and if nothing changed the server answers 304 Not Modified without a body. TypedRest then returns the entity it kept from before.

GET /contacts/1337                                →  200 OK, ETag: "v7"
PUT /contacts/1337, If-Match: "v7"  (Alice)       →  204 No Content
PUT /contacts/1337, If-Match: "v7"  (Bob)         →  412 Precondition Failed

docs.title: Detecting conflicts
docs.text:
The exception for 412 Precondition Failed is:

.NET Java/Kotlin TypeScript InvalidOperationException ConflictException ConcurrencyError

The example below plays both Alice and Bob, using two endpoint objects for the same contact:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var alice = client.Contacts["1337"];
var bob = client.Contacts["1337"];

var aliceCopy = await alice.ReadAsync(); // ETag "v7"
var bobCopy = await bob.ReadAsync();     // ETag "v7"

aliceCopy.Email = "smith@example.com";
await alice.SetAsync(aliceCopy);         // If-Match: "v7", succeeds

bobCopy.Name = "Smith";
try
{
    await bob.SetAsync(bobCopy);         // If-Match: "v7", fails
}
catch (InvalidOperationException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Someone else changed this contact. Please review their changes.");
}

ContactEndpoint alice = client.getContacts().get("1337");
ContactEndpoint bob = client.getContacts().get("1337");

Contact aliceCopy = alice.read(); // ETag "v7"
Contact bobCopy = bob.read();     // ETag "v7"

aliceCopy.setEmail("smith@example.com");
alice.set(aliceCopy);             // If-Match: "v7", succeeds

bobCopy.setName("Smith");
try {
    bob.set(bobCopy);             // If-Match: "v7", fails
} catch (ConflictException ex) {
    System.out.println("Someone else changed this contact. Please review their changes.");
}

val alice = client.contacts["1337"]
val bob = client.contacts["1337"]

val aliceCopy = alice.read() // ETag "v7"
val bobCopy = bob.read()     // ETag "v7"

alice.set(aliceCopy.copy(email = "smith@example.com")) // If-Match: "v7", succeeds

try {
    bob.set(bobCopy.copy(name = "Smith"))              // If-Match: "v7", fails
} catch (ex: ConflictException) {
    println("Someone else changed this contact. Please review their changes.")
}

import { ConcurrencyError } from "typedrest/errors";

const alice = client.contacts.get("1337");
const bob = client.contacts.get("1337");

const aliceCopy = await alice.read(); // ETag "v7"
const bobCopy = await bob.read();     // ETag "v7"

aliceCopy.email = "smith@example.com";
await alice.set(aliceCopy);           // If-Match: "v7", succeeds

bobCopy.name = "Smith";
try {
    await bob.set(bobCopy);           // If-Match: "v7", fails
} catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof ConcurrencyError) console.log("Someone else changed this contact. Please review their changes.");
    else throw err;
}

In .NET and Java/Kotlin the same exception type is also used for 409 Conflict. In Java/Kotlin you can tell them apart by the exception's status. In .NET, derive from DefaultErrorHandler and override MapException if you need a separate exception type for 412, then pass your handler to the entry endpoint's constructor.

Keep the endpoint object

The ETag is stored in the endpoint object that did the read. This sends no If-Match:

var contact = await client.Contacts["1337"].ReadAsync();
contact.Name = "Smith";
await client.Contacts["1337"].SetAsync(contact); // a new endpoint object, which has never read anything

Keep the endpoint in a variable for the whole read-modify-write cycle, as in the examples above.

Every set or delete clears the stored response before sending its request. After catching the 412 above, bob therefore has no ETag left: calling bob.SetAsync(bobCopy) again would send no If-Match and overwrite Alice's change after all. Always read again before the next set, or use update as described below.

docs.title: Retrying automatically
docs.text:
Often the right reaction to a conflict is simply to start over: read the current version, apply the same change to it, and try to save again. The update method does exactly that, up to a maximum number of retries (3 by default):

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
await client.Contacts["1337"].UpdateAsync(contact => contact.Name = "Smith");

There are overloads taking a Func<Contact, Contact> and a maximum number of retries. If the server sends a Retry-After header with the 412, TypedRest waits that long before retrying.

client.getContacts().get("1337").update(contact -> {
    contact.setName("Smith");
    return contact;
}, 3);

If the server sends a Retry-After header with the 412, TypedRest waits that long before retrying.

client.contacts["1337"].update({ it.copy(name = "Smith") })

If the server sends a Retry-After header with the 412, TypedRest waits that long before retrying.

await client.contacts.get("1337").update(contact => { contact.name = "Smith"; });

TypedRest for TypeScript retries immediately, without waiting for a Retry-After delay.

The change you pass in may run more than once, so it must only depend on the entity it receives, not on state that changes between calls.

If all retries fail, the last exception is thrown.

docs.title: JSON Patch (.NET only)
docs.text:
.NET also offers an UpdateAsync overload that takes a JSON Patch document. It sends only the change, as a PATCH request with the content type application/json-patch+json, so there is no stale copy that could overwrite someone else's change:

await client.Contacts["1337"].UpdateAsync(patch => patch.Replace(x => x.Name, "Smith"));

If the server does not support JSON Patch and answers 404 Not Found or 405 Method Not Allowed, TypedRest falls back to the read-modify-write cycle.

docs.title: Merge is not protected
docs.text: merge (PATCH with a partial entity) sends no If-Match. It does not need to, as long as the server only changes the fields present in the request. Use it for changes that should win no matter what else happened to the entity, and set or update for changes that depend on the version you read.

docs.title: What the server needs to do
docs.text:
TypedRest only sends conditional requests if the server cooperates:

  • Send an ETag header on GET responses for the elements you want to protect. Any string that changes whenever the entity changes will do: a version number, a timestamp or a hash of the content.
  • Check If-Match on PUT and DELETE. If the header is present and does not match the current ETag, respond with 412 Precondition Failed and change nothing.
  • Check If-None-Match on GET and respond with 304 Not Modified if it matches. This is optional; it only saves bandwidth.
  • Do not send Cache-Control: no-store on those responses. TypedRest for .NET and Java/Kotlin does not keep responses marked like this, so it would have no ETag to send.

In .NET and Java/Kotlin, a Last-Modified header works as a fallback when there is no ETag: TypedRest then sends If-Unmodified-Since and If-Modified-Since instead. Timestamps have a resolution of one second, so prefer ETags if changes can happen faster than that. TypedRest for TypeScript only supports ETags.

docs.title: Dependency injection
docs.text:
In a service or web application you usually don't create clients by hand. You register them with the dependency injection container once, configure the HTTP client there, and let the container pass the client to whatever needs it.

This tutorial registers the AddressBookClient from Build your first client in ASP.NET Core.

docs.title: ASP.NET Core
docs.text: Everything in this section works for any .NET application that uses IServiceCollection, such as worker services or console apps built on the generic host.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the client
docs.text:
AddTypedRest() registers the client as a typed HTTP client: IHttpClientFactory creates and configures the HttpClient and passes it to the client's constructor, so the client needs a constructor that takes one (see Dependency injection in the .NET reference). An interface makes it easy to replace the client in tests:

public interface IAddressBookClient : IEndpoint
{
    ICollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint> Contacts { get; }
}

public class AddressBookClient : EntryEndpoint, IAddressBookClient
{
    // For use without dependency injection
    public AddressBookClient(Uri uri) : base(uri) {}

    // For AddTypedRest(), which sets HttpClient.BaseAddress to the API's URI
    public AddressBookClient(HttpClient httpClient) : base(httpClient) {}

    public ICollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint> Contacts
        => new CollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint>(this, relativeUri: "./contacts");
}

To mock calls deeper in the client, such as Contacts["1337"].Poke, give ContactEndpoint an interface as well; see Mocking a custom client. If you generate the client, it already has interfaces for everything, and you can add the constructor in a partial class.

docs.title: 2. Register the client
docs.text:
Put the API's URI in appsettings.json:

{
  "AddressBook": {
    "Uri": "https://example.com/api/"
  }
}

and register the client in Program.cs:

builder.Services.AddTypedRest<IAddressBookClient, AddressBookClient>(
    new Uri(builder.Configuration["AddressBook:Uri"]!));

docs.title: 3. Use the client
docs.text:
Ask for IAddressBookClient wherever you need it, for example in a minimal API handler:

app.MapGet("/team", async (IAddressBookClient addressBook, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
{
    var contacts = await addressBook.Contacts.ReadAllAsync(cancellationToken);
    return contacts.Select(x => x.Name);
});

or in the constructor of a service:

public class TeamService(IAddressBookClient addressBook)
{
    public async Task WelcomeAsync(string contactId, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
        => await addressBook.Contacts[contactId].Poke.InvokeAsync(cancellationToken);
}

The client is registered as transient. Do not keep it in a singleton for the lifetime of the application; the reference explains why and what to do instead.

docs.title: 4. Configure the HTTP client
docs.text:
AddTypedRest() returns an IHttpClientBuilder, so all of the HTTP client configuration that ASP.NET Core offers is available. For example, to set a timeout and add retries for transient errors with Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience:

var uri = new Uri(builder.Configuration["AddressBook:Uri"]!);

builder.Services.AddTypedRest<IAddressBookClient, AddressBookClient>(uri)
    .ConfigureHttpClient(x => x.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler(options => options.Retry.DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods());

DisableForUnsafeHttpMethods() turns off retries for POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and CONNECT, so only reads such as GET are repeated. Without it, a POST that reached the server but whose response got lost would be sent again and could create a contact twice.

docs.title: 5. Add authentication
docs.text:
For HTTP Basic authentication:

builder.Services.AddTypedRest<IAddressBookClient, AddressBookClient>(uri)
    .AddBasicAuth(credentials => builder.Configuration.GetSection("AddressBook:Credentials").Bind(credentials));

For OAuth 2.0, add TypedRest.OAuth and its handler, which requests tokens with the client credentials flow and renews them before they expire:

builder.Services.AddTypedRest<IAddressBookClient, AddressBookClient>(uri)
    .AddOAuthHandler(options => builder.Configuration.GetSection("AddressBook:OAuth").Bind(options));

{
  "AddressBook": {
    "Uri": "https://example.com/api/",
    "OAuth": {
      "Uri": "https://identity.example.com/",
      "ClientId": "address-book-sync",
      "Scope": "contacts"
    }
  }
}

Keep the client secret out of appsettings.json. Set AddressBook:OAuth:ClientSecret with user secrets during development and with an environment variable (AddressBook__OAuth__ClientSecret) or a secret store in production.

Each registered client gets its own options, so several clients in one application can authenticate against different identity servers.

docs.title: Next steps

docs.title: Build your first client
docs.text:
This tutorial builds a client for the example address book API by hand. It starts with a single collection and grows into a client class that mirrors the API's URL structure, so the code that uses it reads like the API itself:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
await client.Contacts["1337"].Note.SetAsync(new Note { Content = "Call back on Monday" });

client.getContacts().get("1337").getNote().set(new Note("Call back on Monday"));

client.contacts["1337"].note.set(Note("Call back on Monday"))

await client.contacts.get("1337").note.set({ content: "Call back on Monday" });

If your API has an OpenAPI document, you can generate the client instead. Reading this tutorial first still helps you understand what the generator produces.

docs.title: 1. Install TypedRest
docs.text: Follow the setup guide for your language and add the entity classes to your project.

docs.title: 2. Talk to a collection
docs.text:
Every client starts with an entry endpoint for the API's base URI. Other endpoints are created relative to it. Before writing any classes, try a collection endpoint directly:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var client = new EntryEndpoint(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"));
var contacts = new CollectionEndpoint<Contact>(client, relativeUri: "./contacts");

// GET /api/contacts
List<Contact> all = await contacts.ReadAllAsync();

// POST /api/contacts
var smith = await contacts.CreateAsync(new Contact { Name = "Smith" });

// GET /api/contacts/{id}, using the URI from the Location header
Contact contact = await smith!.ReadAsync();

Without a Location header, TypedRest only finds the ID in the response body if the entity has a property marked with [Key] (from System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations). The Contact class above has no such attribute, so for it TypedRest relies on the Location header alone. Add [Key] to Id if your server returns the new entity without a Location header.

EntryEndpoint client = new EntryEndpoint(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"), (HttpCredentials) null, new JacksonJsonSerializer());
CollectionEndpoint<Contact> contacts = new CollectionEndpointImpl<>(client, "./contacts", Contact.class);

// GET /api/contacts
List<Contact> all = contacts.readAll();

// POST /api/contacts
ElementEndpoint<Contact> smith = contacts.create(new Contact("Smith"));

// GET /api/contacts/{id}, using the URI from the Location header
Contact contact = smith.read();

Without a Location header, TypedRest finds the ID in the response body by calling the entity's getId() method.

val client = EntryEndpoint(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"))
val contacts = CollectionEndpointImpl(client, "./contacts", Contact::class.java)

// GET /api/contacts
val all = contacts.readAll()

// POST /api/contacts
val smith = contacts.create(Contact(name = "Smith"))

// GET /api/contacts/{id}, using the URI from the Location header
val contact = smith!!.read()

Without a Location header, TypedRest finds the ID in the response body by calling the entity's getId() method, which Kotlin generates for the id property.

const client = new EntryEndpoint(new URL("https://example.com/api/"));
const contacts = new CollectionEndpoint<Contact>(client, "./contacts");

// GET /api/contacts
const all = await contacts.readAll();

// POST /api/contacts
const smith = await contacts.create({ name: "Smith" });

// GET /api/contacts/{id}, using the URI from the Location header
const contact = await smith!.read();

Without a Location header, TypedRest finds the ID in the response body by reading the entity's id property.

Creating an element returns an endpoint for it rather than the entity. TypedRest takes the new element's URI from the Location header, or from the ID in the response body if there is no such header. If the server sends neither, it returns null/undefined, which is why the code above needs ! or !!.

The ./ prefix

./contacts resolves to https://example.com/api/contacts. Without the ./, URI resolution would replace the last segment of the parent URI if it lacked a trailing slash. Prefixing relative URIs with ./ makes child URIs predictable. See Relative URIs.

docs.title: 3. Wrap it in a client class
docs.text:
Creating endpoints inline works, but every caller would need to know the URL structure. Instead, derive from the entry endpoint and expose child endpoints as properties:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
public class AddressBookClient(Uri uri) : EntryEndpoint(uri)
{
    public CollectionEndpoint<Contact> Contacts => new(this, relativeUri: "./contacts");
}

public class AddressBookClient extends EntryEndpoint {
    public AddressBookClient(URI uri) {
        super(uri, (HttpCredentials) null, new JacksonJsonSerializer());
    }

    public CollectionEndpoint<Contact> getContacts() {
        return new CollectionEndpointImpl<>(this, "./contacts", Contact.class);
    }
}

class AddressBookClient(uri: URI) : EntryEndpoint(uri) {
    val contacts: CollectionEndpoint<Contact>
        get() = CollectionEndpointImpl(this, "./contacts", Contact::class.java)
}

import { EntryEndpoint } from "typedrest/endpoints";
import { CollectionEndpoint } from "typedrest/endpoints/generic";

export class AddressBookClient extends EntryEndpoint {
    get contacts() {
        return new CollectionEndpoint<Contact>(this, "./contacts");
    }
}

Each access to the property creates a new endpoint object. That is cheap, because an endpoint is only a URI plus a reference to its parent; the HTTP client, serializer and error handler are shared with the entry endpoint.

docs.title: 4. Add sub-resources
docs.text:
A contact has a note and a poke action, but CollectionEndpoint<Contact> hands out plain element endpoints that know nothing about them. Derive your own element endpoint and tell the collection to use it:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
public class ContactEndpoint(IEndpoint referrer, Uri relativeUri)
    : ElementEndpoint<Contact>(referrer, relativeUri)
{
    public ElementEndpoint<Note> Note => new(this, relativeUri: "./note");

    public ActionEndpoint Poke => new(this, relativeUri: "./poke");
}

public class AddressBookClient(Uri uri) : EntryEndpoint(uri)
{
    public CollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint> Contacts => new(this, relativeUri: "./contacts");
}

The collection creates element endpoints through a constructor with exactly the signature (IEndpoint referrer, Uri relativeUri), so keep it.

public class ContactEndpoint extends ElementEndpointImpl<Contact> {
    public ContactEndpoint(Endpoint referrer, URI relativeUri) {
        super(referrer, relativeUri, Contact.class);
    }

    public ElementEndpoint<Note> getNote() {
        return new ElementEndpointImpl<>(this, "./note", Note.class);
    }

    public ActionEndpoint getPoke() {
        return new ActionEndpointImpl(this, "./poke");
    }
}

public class AddressBookClient extends EntryEndpoint {
    public AddressBookClient(URI uri) {
        super(uri, (HttpCredentials) null, new JacksonJsonSerializer());
    }

    public GenericCollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint> getContacts() {
        return new GenericCollectionEndpointImpl<>(this, "./contacts", Contact.class, ContactEndpoint::new);
    }
}

class ContactEndpoint(referrer: Endpoint, relativeUri: URI) :
    ElementEndpointImpl<Contact>(referrer, relativeUri, Contact::class.java) {
    val note: ElementEndpoint<Note>
        get() = ElementEndpointImpl(this, "./note", Note::class.java)

    val poke: ActionEndpoint
        get() = ActionEndpointImpl(this, "./poke")
}

class AddressBookClient(uri: URI) : EntryEndpoint(uri) {
    val contacts: GenericCollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint>
        get() = GenericCollectionEndpointImpl(this, "./contacts", Contact::class.java, ::ContactEndpoint)
}

import { EntryEndpoint } from "typedrest/endpoints";
import { ElementEndpoint, GenericCollectionEndpoint } from "typedrest/endpoints/generic";
import { ActionEndpoint } from "typedrest/endpoints/rpc";

export class ContactEndpoint extends ElementEndpoint<Contact> {
    get note() {
        return new ElementEndpoint<Note>(this, "./note");
    }

    get poke() {
        return new ActionEndpoint(this, "./poke");
    }
}

export class AddressBookClient extends EntryEndpoint {
    get contacts() {
        return new GenericCollectionEndpoint<Contact, ContactEndpoint>(this, "./contacts", ContactEndpoint);
    }
}

The note is an element endpoint because it can be read and replaced. Poking is not a resource at all, just something the server does, so it is an action endpoint. TypedRest has an endpoint type for each of these common shapes; see Endpoints for the full list.

docs.title: 5. Use the client
docs.text:
The client now covers the whole API:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var client = new AddressBookClient(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"));

// POST /api/contacts -> Location: /api/contacts/1337
ContactEndpoint smith = (await client.Contacts.CreateAsync(new Contact { Name = "Smith" }))!;

// PUT /api/contacts/1337/note
await smith.Note.SetAsync(new Note { Content = "Call back on Monday" });

// POST /api/contacts/1337/poke
await smith.Poke.InvokeAsync();

// Address an existing contact by ID
Note note = await client.Contacts["1337"].Note.ReadAsync();

// DELETE /api/contacts/1337
await smith.DeleteAsync();

AddressBookClient client = new AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"));

// POST /api/contacts -> Location: /api/contacts/1337
ContactEndpoint smith = client.getContacts().create(new Contact("Smith"));

// PUT /api/contacts/1337/note
smith.getNote().set(new Note("Call back on Monday"));

// POST /api/contacts/1337/poke
smith.getPoke().invoke();

// Address an existing contact by ID
Note note = client.getContacts().get("1337").getNote().read();

// DELETE /api/contacts/1337
smith.delete();

val client = AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"))

// POST /api/contacts -> Location: /api/contacts/1337
val smith = client.contacts.create(Contact(name = "Smith"))!!

// PUT /api/contacts/1337/note
smith.note.set(Note("Call back on Monday"))

// POST /api/contacts/1337/poke
smith.poke.invoke()

// Address an existing contact by ID
val note = client.contacts["1337"].note.read()

// DELETE /api/contacts/1337
smith.delete()

const client = new AddressBookClient(new URL("https://example.com/api/"));

// POST /api/contacts -> Location: /api/contacts/1337
const smith = (await client.contacts.create({ name: "Smith" }))!;

// PUT /api/contacts/1337/note
await smith.note.set({ content: "Call back on Monday" });

// POST /api/contacts/1337/poke
await smith.poke.invoke();

// Address an existing contact by ID
const note = await client.contacts.get("1337").note.read();

// DELETE /api/contacts/1337
await smith.delete();

client.Contacts["1337"] does not send a request. Building endpoints is purely local; a request goes out only when you call a method such as read or set.

docs.title: 6. Handle errors
docs.text:
When the server responds with an error status, TypedRest throws an exception (or rejects the promise) of a type that matches the status code. A missing contact, for example:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
try
{
    var contact = await client.Contacts["999"].ReadAsync();
}
catch (KeyNotFoundException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("No such contact");
}

try {
    Contact contact = client.getContacts().get("999").read();
} catch (NotFoundException ex) {
    System.out.println("No such contact");
}

try {
    val contact = client.contacts["999"].read()
} catch (ex: NotFoundException) {
    println("No such contact")
}

import { NotFoundError } from "typedrest/errors";

try {
    const contact = await client.contacts.get("999").read();
} catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof NotFoundError) console.log("No such contact");
    else throw err;
}

If the response body is JSON with a message or details field, its text becomes the exception message. See Error handling for the full mapping of status codes.

docs.text:
• Authentication: add credentials or tokens to the client.
  • Testing your client: check that the endpoints send the requests you expect.
  • Endpoints: the other endpoint types you can use for the rest of your API.

docs.title: Generate a client from OpenAPI
docs.text:
If your API has an OpenAPI document, TypedRest can write the client for you. This tutorial takes a spec for the example address book API, generates a client from it, fixes an endpoint the generator could not have known about, and adds hand-written code on top.

The Code generation section describes each tool in detail. This page shows how they fit together.

docs.title: 1. The spec
docs.text:
Save this as addressbook.yml. Besides the paths from the example API it has one more: /contacts/{id}/events, which pushes a contact's changes as Server-Sent Events.

openapi: 3.0.1
info:
  title: Address Book
  version: '1.0'
paths:
  /contacts:
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          description: All contacts
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/Contact'
    post:
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/Contact'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Created
  '/contacts/{id}':
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A contact
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Contact'
    put:
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/Contact'
      responses:
        '204':
          description: Updated
    delete:
      responses:
        '204':
          description: Deleted
  '/contacts/{id}/note':
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          description: The note attached to a contact
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Note'
    put:
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/Note'
      responses:
        '204':
          description: Updated
  '/contacts/{id}/poke':
    post:
      responses:
        '204':
          description: Poked
  '/contacts/{id}/events':
    get:
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Changes to a contact as Server-Sent Events
          content:
            text/event-stream:
              schema:
                type: string
components:
  schemas:
    Contact:
      type: object
      required: [name]
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
        name:
          type: string
        email:
          type: string
    Note:
      type: object
      properties:
        content:
          type: string
    ContactEvent:
      type: object
      properties:
        type:
          type: string
        contact:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/Contact'

docs.title: 2. Install the tool
docs.text:
dotnet tool install -g typedrest-codegen

The command-line tool needs the .NET SDK to run, but it can generate clients in every language. C# projects can use the source generator instead, which is introduced in step 5. Install the CLI anyway, since step 3 uses it to inspect the inference.

docs.title: 3. Check what the generator infers
docs.text:
The generator does not translate paths one by one. It matches each path against patterns such as "a GET returning an array, plus a child path returning one element of it is a collection". Before generating code, look at the result of that step:

typedrest-codegen pattern -f addressbook.yml

This writes the inferred structure back into addressbook.yml as an x-typedrest extension:

x-typedrest:
  contacts:
    kind: collection
    uri: ./contacts
    description: All contacts
    schema:
      $ref: '#/components/schemas/Contact'
    element:
      kind: element
      description: A contact
      children:
        note:
          kind: element
          uri: ./note
          description: The note attached to a contact
          schema:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Note'
        poke:
          kind: action
          uri: ./poke
          description: Poked
        events:
          kind: blob
          uri: ./events
          description: Changes to a contact as Server-Sent Events

The descriptions are taken from the spec and end up as documentation comments in the generated code.

Run pattern only once

pattern always runs the inference again and replaces any x-typedrest already in the document. Running it after the edit in the next step would undo that edit. It also rewrites the whole file in a normalized form, so commit the spec before running it if you want to review the changes.

/contacts became a collection whose elements have a note element and a poke action, as intended. But events became a blob endpoint: its response is not JSON, and an OpenAPI document cannot say that a response is a stream of entities rather than a file to download.

docs.title: 4. Fix the inference
docs.text:
Edit the events entry by hand to make it an SSE endpoint that delivers ContactEvent entities:

        events:
          kind: sse
          uri: ./events
          description: Changes to a contact as Server-Sent Events
          schema:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/ContactEvent'

When a document contains x-typedrest, the code generator (the generate command and the source generator) uses it as-is instead of running the inference again, so your edit survives every regeneration of the client. It also means that paths you add to the spec later have to be added to the extension too. Custom code explains this and lists every kind and its properties.

docs.title: 5. Generate the client
docs.text:
C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

Add the source generator and the libraries the generated code depends on. The generated events endpoint needs TypedRest.Reactive:

dotnet add package TypedRest.SourceGenerator
dotnet add package TypedRest
dotnet add package TypedRest.Reactive

Reference the spec in your project file:

<ItemGroup>
  <TypedRestOpenApi Include="addressbook.yml" ServiceName="AddressBook" Namespace="MyCompany.AddressBook" />
</ItemGroup>

The client is generated on every build, together with interfaces and DTO classes. Set <EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>true</EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles> if you want to read the generated files in obj/.

If you would rather check the generated code in, use the CLI instead:

typedrest-codegen generate -f addressbook.yml -o AddressBook/ -s AddressBook -n MyCompany.AddressBook --generate-interfaces --generate-dtos

typedrest-codegen generate -l java -f addressbook.yml -o src/main/java/ -s AddressBook -n com.mycompany.addressbook --generate-dtos

Add the net.typedrest:typedrest, net.typedrest:typedrest-serializers-jackson and net.typedrest:typedrest-reactive dependencies, plus org.jspecify:jspecify for the nullability annotations on the DTOs.

typedrest-codegen generate -l kotlin -f addressbook.yml -o src/main/kotlin/ -s AddressBook -n com.mycompany.addressbook --generate-dtos

Add the net.typedrest:typedrest and net.typedrest:typedrest-reactive dependencies. The DTOs are annotated for kotlinx.serialization, so you also need the kotlin("plugin.serialization") Gradle plugin and an explicit org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-serialization-json dependency.

typedrest-codegen generate -l typescript -f addressbook.yml -o src/addressbook/ -s AddressBook --generate-dtos

Run npm install typedrest. Reactive endpoints are part of the main package.

The command-line tool page lists all options, including how to pick a different serializer for the DTOs.

docs.title: 6. Use the generated client
docs.text:
The service name AddressBook produces an entry endpoint called AddressBookClient. The collection becomes a Contacts property, its elements are ContactElementEndpoints, and the children are named after their path segments:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
using MyCompany.AddressBook;

var client = new AddressBookClient(new Uri("https://example.com/api/"));

var smith = (await client.Contacts.CreateAsync(new Contact { Name = "Smith" }))!;
await smith.Note.SetAsync(new Note { Content = "Call back on Monday" });
await smith.Poke.InvokeAsync();

// Print every change to the contact as it happens
smith.Events.GetObservable().Subscribe(x => Console.WriteLine($"{x.Type}: {x.Contact?.Name}"));

AddressBookClient client = new AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"));

Contact contact = new Contact();
contact.name = "Smith";
ContactElementEndpoint smith = client.getContacts().create(contact);
smith.getNote().set(new Note("Call back on Monday"));
smith.getPoke().invoke();

// Print every change to the contact as it happens
smith.getEvents().getObservable().subscribe(
    x -> System.out.println(x.type + ": " + (x.contact == null ? null : x.contact.name)),
    Throwable::printStackTrace);

Generated Java DTOs have public fields; see Command-line tool for what else they look like.

val client = AddressBookClient(URI.create("https://example.com/api/"))

val smith = client.contacts.create(Contact(name = "Smith"))!!
smith.note.set(Note(content = "Call back on Monday"))
smith.poke.invoke()

// Print every change to the contact as it happens
smith.events.getObservable().subscribe { println("${it.type}: ${it.contact?.name}") }

import { AddressBookClient } from "./addressbook";

const client = new AddressBookClient("https://example.com/api/");

const smith = (await client.contacts.create({ name: "Smith" }))!;
await smith.note.set({ content: "Call back on Monday" });
await smith.poke.invoke();

// Print every change to the contact as it happens
for await (const x of smith.events.stream()) {
    console.log(`${x.type}: ${x.contact?.name}`);
}

Compare this with the hand-written client: the structure is the same, only the class names differ.

docs.title: 7. Add your own code
docs.text:
Generated code is regenerated, so do not edit it. Add to it instead, as described in Extend the generated code:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript

Add to the partial class and its partial interface in a file of your own. The collection hands out elements as IContactElementEndpoint, so a method that is only on the class would not be reachable from client.Contacts["1337"]:

namespace MyCompany.AddressBook;

public partial interface IContactElementEndpoint
{
    /// <summary>
    /// Changes the name of the contact, retrying if someone else modified it in the meantime.
    /// </summary>
    Task<Contact?> RenameAsync(string name, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
}

public partial class ContactElementEndpoint
{
    public Task<Contact?> RenameAsync(string name, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
        => UpdateAsync(contact => contact.Name = name, cancellationToken: cancellationToken);
}

await client.Contacts["1337"].RenameAsync("Smith");

Derive from the generated class:

public class MyAddressBookClient extends AddressBookClient {
    public MyAddressBookClient(URI uri) {
        super(uri);
    }

    public List<Contact> findByName(String name) {
        return getContacts().readAll().stream()
            .filter(x -> x.name.equals(name))
            .toList();
    }
}

Derive from the generated class, or use an extension function:

fun AddressBookClient.findByName(name: String) = contacts.readAll().filter { it.name == name }

Derive from the generated class:

export class MyAddressBookClient extends AddressBookClient {
    async findByName(name: string) {
        return (await this.contacts.readAll()).filter(x => x.name === name);
    }
}

RenameAsync uses a read-modify-write cycle with ETags; see Optimistic concurrency.

docs.title: Keeping client and spec in sync
docs.text: The source generator picks up a changed spec on the next build, while the CLI has to be rerun (details). Either way, paths added to the spec must also be added to x-typedrest, as described in step 4.

  • Live updates: more about the SSE endpoint used for events.

docs.title: Live updates
docs.text:
Sometimes reading a resource once is not enough: you want to know when it changes. TypedRest has four reactive endpoint types for this. Each one turns repeated or long-running HTTP requests into a stream of entities, but they put different demands on the server.

This tutorial uses each of them for a different part of the address book: an import job you wait for, a change log you follow, and events the server pushes.

Packages

For .NET, add the TypedRest.Reactive NuGet package. For Java/Kotlin, add the typedrest-reactive Maven artifact. In TypeScript, reactive endpoints are part of the main typedrest package. .NET and Java/Kotlin provide streams as observables, TypeScript as async iterables; see Reactive endpoints.

docs.title: Wait for a job to finish: polling
docs.text:
Say the API imports contacts from a file in the background. POST /imports starts an import, and GET /imports/42 returns its current state:

{ "state": "running", "progress": 40 }

The server needs nothing special for this. A polling endpoint reads the resource repeatedly and emits each new state, until the end condition you pass is met:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var job = new PollingEndpoint<ImportJob>(client, "./imports/42", endCondition: x => x.State == "completed")
{
    PollingInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)
};

// Awaiting an observable returns its last element (requires using System.Reactive.Linq)
ImportJob final = await job.GetObservable()
    .Do(x => Console.WriteLine($"{x.Progress}% done"));

PollingEndpointImpl<ImportJob> job = new PollingEndpointImpl<>(client, "./imports/42", ImportJob.class,
    x -> x.getState().equals("completed"));
job.setPollingInterval(Duration.ofSeconds(2));

job.getObservable()
    .blockingForEach(x -> System.out.println(x.getProgress() + "% done"));

val job = PollingEndpointImpl(client, "./imports/42", ImportJob::class.java) { it.state == "completed" }
    .apply { pollingInterval = Duration.ofSeconds(2) }

job.getObservable()
    .blockingForEach { println("${it.progress}% done") }

const job = new PollingEndpoint<ImportJob>(client, "./imports/42", x => x.state === "completed");
job.pollingInterval = 2000;

for await (const x of job.stream()) {
    console.log(`${x.progress}% done`);
}

States identical to the previous one are skipped, so you only see changes. In .NET and Java/Kotlin, give ImportJob value equality for this to work; see Change detection. The server can also slow clients down with a Retry-After header.

A polling endpoint is also an element endpoint, so you can still read, set or delete the job with it.

docs.title: Follow a growing collection: streaming collection
docs.text:
Say the API keeps a log of every change to the address book at /contacts/changes, where new entries are only ever added to the end. A streaming collection endpoint reads the entries that exist and then keeps asking for new ones:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var changes = new StreamingCollectionEndpoint<ContactChange>(client, "./contacts/changes");

// Start with the last 10 entries, then follow new ones
using var subscription = changes.GetObservable(startIndex: -10)
    .Subscribe(x => Console.WriteLine($"{x.Type}: {x.ContactId}"));

StreamingCollectionEndpoint<ContactChange> changes = new StreamingCollectionEndpointImpl<>(client, "./contacts/changes", ContactChange.class);

// Start with the last 10 entries, then follow new ones
Disposable subscription = changes.getObservable(-10)
    .subscribe(x -> System.out.println(x.getType() + ": " + x.getContactId()));

val changes = StreamingCollectionEndpointImpl(client, "./contacts/changes", ContactChange::class.java)

// Start with the last 10 entries, then follow new ones
val subscription = changes.getObservable(-10)
    .subscribe { println("${it.type}: ${it.contactId}") }

const changes = new StreamingCollectionEndpoint<ContactChange>(client, "./contacts/changes");

// Start with the last 10 entries, then follow new ones
for await (const x of changes.stream(-10)) {
    console.log(`${x.type}: ${x.contactId}`);
}

A positive start index skips that many entries instead, which lets a client that has already processed entries resume where it left off.

This uses the same range requests as paging: the client keeps asking for the entries after the last one it has seen, and the server answers 416 Range Not Satisfiable while there are none. Server requirements describes the exchange, including why the server must leave the total out of Content-Range.

The endpoint is still a collection endpoint, so you can also read and create entries with it.

docs.title: Receive pushed events: Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
Polling always lags behind by up to one interval and sends requests even when nothing happens. If the server can keep a connection open and push events as they occur, use Server-Sent Events (SSE), the standard format for this that browsers also understand.

Say GET /contacts/1337/events pushes an event whenever that contact changes. The server responds with Content-Type: text/event-stream and writes events into the open response as they happen:

id: 17
event: updated
data: {"type":"updated","contact":{"id":"1337","name":"Smith"}}

id: 18
event: deleted
data: {"type":"deleted"}

An SSE endpoint deserializes the data of each event as an entity:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var events = new SseStreamingEndpoint<ContactEvent>(client, "./contacts/1337/events");

using var subscription = events.GetObservable()
    .Subscribe(x => Console.WriteLine($"{x.Type}: {x.Contact?.Name}"));

StreamingEndpoint<ContactEvent> events = new SseStreamingEndpointImpl<>(client, "./contacts/1337/events", ContactEvent.class, null);

Disposable subscription = events.getObservable()
    .subscribe(x -> System.out.println(x.getType()));

val events = SseStreamingEndpointImpl(client, "./contacts/1337/events", ContactEvent::class.java)

val subscription = events.getObservable()
    .subscribe { println("${it.type}: ${it.contact?.name}") }

const events = new SseStreamingEndpoint<ContactEvent>(client, "./contacts/1337/events");

for await (const x of events.stream()) {
    console.log(`${x.type}: ${x.contact?.name}`);
}

If the connection drops, the endpoint reconnects on its own and sends the id of the last event it received as a Last-Event-ID header, so a server that keeps recent events can send the ones the client missed.

To receive only some kinds of events, pass an event type to the constructor; events with a different event: field are then ignored.

If your server streams entities without the SSE format, for example as newline-delimited JSON, use a streaming endpoint instead. It splits the response body on a separator, but has no event types, IDs or reconnecting.

docs.title: Stopping a stream
docs.text: In .NET and Java/Kotlin, dispose the subscription; the C# examples above do this with using when the variable goes out of scope. In TypeScript, break out of the loop. To stop a TypeScript stream from somewhere else, pass an AbortSignal; see Stopping a stream.

docs.title: Choosing an endpoint
docs.text: As a rule of thumb: use polling if you cannot change the server, a streaming collection if the data is a list that only grows and clients need to catch up on what they missed, and SSE if updates must arrive immediately. Choosing an endpoint compares all four reactive endpoints, including what each needs from your infrastructure.

docs.title: Paging
docs.text: Reading all ten thousand contacts with a single GET /contacts is slow and memory-hungry. Many APIs let clients fetch a collection in pages instead. TypedRest uses the standard HTTP mechanism for this, range requests, applied to elements of a collection instead of bytes of a file.

docs.title: The protocol
docs.text:
The client asks for a range of elements with a Range header. Positions start at 0 and both ends are inclusive:

GET /contacts
Range: elements=0-49

The server responds with 206 Partial Content, the requested elements, and a Content-Range header saying which elements these are and how many there are in total:

HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content
Content-Range: elements 0-49/1234
Content-Type: application/json

[ ...50 contacts... ]

If the start of the requested range lies beyond the end of the collection, the server responds with 416 Range Not Satisfiable.

To tell clients that it supports this, the server includes Accept-Ranges: elements in its responses for the collection.

docs.title: Reading one page
docs.text:
Collection endpoints have a read range method that returns a PartialResponse. It contains the elements, the range they came from, and whether the end of the collection was reached:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
PartialResponse<Contact> page = await client.Contacts.ReadRangeAsync(new RangeItemHeaderValue(0, 49));

foreach (var contact in page.Elements)
    Console.WriteLine(contact.Name);

Console.WriteLine($"Elements {page.Range?.From}-{page.Range?.To} of {page.Range?.Length}");
bool more = !page.EndReached;

PartialResponse<Contact> page = client.getContacts().readRange(0L, 49L);

for (Contact contact : page.getElements())
    System.out.println(contact.getName());

HttpContentRangeHeader range = page.getRange();
System.out.println("Elements " + range.getFrom() + "-" + range.getTo() + " of " + range.getLength());
boolean more = !page.getEndReached();

val page = client.contacts.readRange(0, 49)

for (contact in page.elements)
    println(contact.name)

println("Elements ${page.range?.from}-${page.range?.to} of ${page.range?.length}")
val more = !page.endReached

const page = await client.contacts.readRange(0, 49);

for (const contact of page.elements)
    console.log(contact.name);

console.log(`Elements ${page.range?.from}-${page.range?.to} of ${page.range?.length}`);
const more = !page.endReached;

EndReached is true when the last element of the page is the last element of the collection. It is also true when the server ignored the Range header and sent the whole collection with 200 OK, so code that pages through a collection works with servers that do not support ranges too.

docs.title: Reading all pages
docs.text:
To process a large collection one page at a time, keep asking for the range after the last one you received. Wrapping this in a function that returns a lazy sequence keeps the paging out of the calling code:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
// In a static class
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<TEntity> ReadAllPagedAsync<TEntity, TElementEndpoint>(
    this ICollectionEndpoint<TEntity, TElementEndpoint> collection,
    long pageSize = 50,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    where TEntity : class
    where TElementEndpoint : IElementEndpoint<TEntity>
{
    long from = 0;
    while (true)
    {
        var page = await collection.ReadRangeAsync(new RangeItemHeaderValue(from, from + pageSize - 1), cancellationToken);
        foreach (var entity in page.Elements)
            yield return entity;

        if (page.EndReached) yield break;
        from = page.Range!.To!.Value + 1;
    }
}

await foreach (var contact in client.Contacts.ReadAllPagedAsync())
    Console.WriteLine(contact.Name);

public static <T> void forEachPaged(GenericCollectionEndpoint<T, ?> collection, long pageSize, Consumer<T> action) {
    long from = 0;
    while (true) {
        PartialResponse<T> page = collection.readRange(from, from + pageSize - 1);
        page.getElements().forEach(action);

        if (page.getEndReached()) return;
        from = page.getRange().getTo() + 1;
    }
}

forEachPaged(client.getContacts(), 50, contact -> System.out.println(contact.getName()));

fun <T> GenericCollectionEndpoint<T, *>.readAllPaged(pageSize: Long = 50): Sequence<T> = sequence {
    var from = 0L
    while (true) {
        val page = readRange(from, from + pageSize - 1)
        yieldAll(page.elements)

        if (page.endReached) break
        from = page.range!!.to!! + 1
    }
}

for (contact in client.contacts.readAllPaged())
    println(contact.name)

import { GenericCollectionEndpoint, ElementEndpoint } from "typedrest/endpoints/generic";

export async function* readAllPaged<T, E extends ElementEndpoint<T>>(collection: GenericCollectionEndpoint<T, E>, pageSize = 50) {
    let from = 0;
    while (true) {
        const page = await collection.readRange(from, from + pageSize - 1);
        yield* page.elements;

        if (page.endReached) return;
        from = page.range!.to! + 1;
    }
}

for await (const contact of readAllPaged(client.contacts))
    console.log(contact.name);

The next page starts after the last element the server actually returned, not after the last one requested. Servers may return smaller pages than asked for, for example to enforce a maximum page size, and this way nothing is skipped.

Pages are fetched only as the loop needs them. Stopping the loop early stops fetching.

Collections that change while you page

Range requests address elements by position. If a contact is inserted or deleted before the current position while you are paging, later pages shift and you may see an element twice or miss one. This is fine for append-only collections and for display purposes. If you need a consistent snapshot, ask for the whole collection in one request.

docs.title: When the server does not send a total
docs.text:
A server may answer with Content-Range: elements 0-49/* if counting all elements is expensive. Then TypedRest cannot tell from the response whether this was the last page, and EndReached stays false. The loop above then requests one range past the end and gets 416 Range Not Satisfiable. Treat that as the end of the collection:

.NET Java/Kotlin TypeScript InvalidOperationException ConflictException RangeNotSatisfiableError C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
PartialResponse<TEntity> page;
try
{
    page = await collection.ReadRangeAsync(new RangeItemHeaderValue(from, from + pageSize - 1), cancellationToken);
}
catch (InvalidOperationException) when (from > 0)
{
    yield break;
}

PartialResponse<T> page;
try {
    page = collection.readRange(from, from + pageSize - 1);
} catch (ConflictException ex) {
    if (from > 0 && ex.getStatus() == HttpStatusCode.RangeNotSatisfiable) return;
    throw ex;
}

val page = try {
    readRange(from, from + pageSize - 1)
} catch (ex: ConflictException) {
    if (from > 0 && ex.status == HttpStatusCode.RangeNotSatisfiable) break
    throw ex
}

import { RangeNotSatisfiableError } from "typedrest/errors";

let page;
try {
    page = await collection.readRange(from, from + pageSize - 1);
} catch (err) {
    if (from > 0 && err instanceof RangeNotSatisfiableError) return;
    throw err;
}

A 416 on the very first page means the collection is empty, which is why the examples only treat it as the end when from > 0. Handle that case too if empty collections are possible.

docs.title: The last few elements
docs.text:
Leave out the start of the range to get the last elements of the collection instead, for example the ten most recently added contacts:

C#JavaKotlinTypeScript 
var latest = await client.Contacts.ReadRangeAsync(new RangeItemHeaderValue(null, 10));

PartialResponse<Contact> latest = client.getContacts().readRange(null, 10L);

val latest = client.contacts.readRange(null, 10)

const latest = await client.contacts.readRange(undefined, 10);

This sends Range: elements=-10. Likewise, leaving out the end (elements=100-) asks for everything from position 100 on.

docs.title: Checking for support
docs.text:
After any request to the collection, the read range allowed property (ReadRangeAllowed in .NET, readRangeAllowed in Java, Kotlin and TypeScript) tells you whether the server sent Accept-Ranges: elements. It is null/undefined before the first request.

If the server uses a different unit name in its Range headers, such as items, change the endpoint's range unit (RangeUnit in .NET, rangeUnit in Java, Kotlin and TypeScript) before sending requests.
